Question 20Incorrect

Pinegrove International runs a REST API on Amazon API Gateway with two stages: test, where the development team validates new features, and prod, which serves live customer traffic. After changes pass validation in test, the team must promote them to prod with minimal disruption. Which solution is optimal?

Delete the existing prod stage, create a new stage with the same name (prod), and deploy the tested version to this new stage

Explanation

Incorrect. Deleting and recreating the prod stage is technically possible. This action causes downtime because prod is a live, customer-facing stage. Deleting the stage also destroys its existing configuration, such as throttling settings and logging, which the team would then have to rebuild manually. Keyword tip: eliminate options that delete a live production resource just to update it; this is rarely the safest deployment method.
Correct answer
Update the stage variable value from the stage name of test to that of prod

Explanation

Correct. A stage variable is a key-value pair that a stage uses to configure parts of its backend integration, such as which Lambda alias or backend endpoint to call. Pinegrove International can update the prod stage's variable to reference the same backend version already validated in the test stage. This promotes the tested build into production without creating a new deployment and without causing downtime. Keyword tip: when a question asks how to promote a stage using a configuration value instead of a full redeployment, think of stage variables.
Deploy the API without choosing a stage; this way, the working deployment will be updated in all stages

Explanation

Incorrect. In Amazon API Gateway, every deployment must target exactly one specific stage. There is no option to deploy without selecting a target stage. Deploying to one stage never updates other stages at the same time. Keyword tip: reject any option that claims one deployment action updates "all stages" simultaneously, since each stage is managed and versioned independently.
Your answer is incorrect
API performance is optimized in a different way for prod environments, so promoting test to prod is not correct; the promotion should be done by redeploying the API to the prod stage

Explanation

Incorrect. The claim that per-stage performance settings block promotion is false. Settings like throttling limits and caching can be changed independently at any time. This option uses an invalid technical justification to argue against a stage-variable-based promotion. Keyword tip: treat any option that declares a feature "not possible" without supporting detail as a likely distractor.

In Amazon API Gateway, a deployment is a snapshot of an API's configuration, and a stage is a named, independently configurable reference to a deployment, such as test or prod. Stage variables are key-value pairs attached to a stage that can point to a specific backend resource, like a Lambda alias or an HTTP endpoint, without embedding that value directly in the API configuration. To promote a tested build to production with no downtime, a team updates the target stage's variable so it references the same validated backend that the source stage already uses, instead of redeploying the API or rebuilding the stage from scratch. Redeploying to the target stage is also a valid promotion technique in other scenarios, but it is not the most efficient option when a stage variable can achieve the same result with less disruption.

Business scenario: Pinegrove International uses its API Gateway prod stage to serve live billing and smart-meter data to municipal water customers, so any downtime directly affects customer-facing services. By updating a stage variable on the prod stage to point to the backend version already validated in test, the development team promotes new billing logic into production instantly and without interrupting active customer requests.

Question 21Incorrect

Palisade Authority's real-time traffic-monitoring platform uses Amazon RDS and must keep its relational database. The agency needs a caching layer supporting geospatial operations, rich queries, and horizontal scaling as sensor coverage grows. Which solution is optimal for this use case?

Your answer is incorrect
Use CloudFront caching to cater to the demands of increasing workloads

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN). CloudFront caches content at edge locations to reduce latency for end users and to offload requests from an origin server. CloudFront works well for static or semi-static content delivery, such as images or web assets. CloudFront does not provide in-memory, sub-millisecond data caching, and CloudFront does not offer geospatial query capabilities for a database tier. Keyword tip: CloudFront solves edge and content delivery caching, not application or database in-memory caching.
Migrate to Amazon DynamoDB to utilize the automatically integrated DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) along with query capability features

Explanation

Incorrect. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB. DAX can reduce DynamoDB read latency from milliseconds to microseconds. This option requires migrating the entire database away from Amazon RDS to DynamoDB. A full database migration is a much larger and more disruptive change than adding a caching layer in front of the existing relational database. Keyword tip: when a question keeps the existing database engine, a full migration option is usually a distractor.
Leverage the capabilities offered by ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode disabled

Explanation

Incorrect. ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode disabled supports only vertical scaling. Vertical scaling means resizing the single primary node to a larger instance type. This configuration also supports up to five read replicas for read scaling. Cluster mode disabled does not support horizontal scaling through sharding, so it cannot meet the stated requirement for horizontal scalability. Keyword tip: cluster mode disabled means vertical scaling only, with a single shard.
Correct answer
Leverage the capabilities offered by ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled

Explanation

Correct. ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled supports horizontal scaling. Horizontal scaling works by adding or removing shards, up to 90 shards. Each shard has its own primary node and up to five read replicas, so both read and write capacity can scale with minimal performance impact. Redis also provides native geospatial commands, such as GEOADD and GEOSEARCH, along with rich query capabilities. These features make cluster mode enabled the best fit for a caching layer that needs geospatial support, query capability, and horizontal scalability. Keyword tip: cluster mode enabled means horizontal scaling through sharding, which fits large-scale geospatial or query-heavy workloads.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon ElastiCache for Redis scaling models and when to choose an in-memory caching layer over other caching or migration strategies. Use ElastiCache for Redis with cluster mode enabled when the workload needs horizontal scalability, geospatial commands, and rich query capability alongside an existing relational database such as Amazon RDS. Use cluster mode disabled only when vertical scaling and simple read replication are enough. Reserve CloudFront for edge and content delivery caching, and consider a database migration such as DynamoDB with DAX only when a full architectural change is justified by the requirements.

Applied example: Palisade Authority can deploy an ElastiCache for Redis cluster with cluster mode enabled in front of its Amazon RDS database to cache location data from traffic sensors across the city. As the agency adds more sensors and intersections to the network, the Redis cluster can add shards to scale horizontally, while Redis geospatial commands let dispatchers quickly query nearby traffic incidents or congestion points. This approach lets the agency keep its existing relational database while adding fast, location-aware caching for a growing sensor network.

Question 22Incorrect

Truenorth Systems uses AWS CodePipeline to automate its release pipelines. The team wants a Lambda function that sends notifications whenever a pipeline state change occurs. Which approach should you recommend to associate the Lambda function with the event source?

Correct answer
Set up an Amazon EventBridge rule that uses CodePipeline as an event source with the target as the Lambda function

Explanation

Correct. Amazon EventBridge can detect state changes in a CodePipeline pipeline, stage, or action. You create an EventBridge rule that uses CodePipeline as the event source and sets the Lambda function as the target. When the pipeline enters the specified state, EventBridge automatically invokes the Lambda function. Keyword tip: when a question describes reacting to state changes in CodePipeline, or in most other AWS services, and invoking a target like Lambda, EventBridge rules are the standard integration pattern.
Set up an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that monitors status changes in CodePipeline and triggers the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudWatch alarms monitor metric thresholds, such as CPU utilization or error counts. CloudWatch alarms do not react to discrete state-change events, such as pipeline, stage, or action transitions in CodePipeline. Detecting these state changes requires an Amazon EventBridge rule, not a CloudWatch alarm. Keyword tip: use CloudWatch alarms for metric-threshold monitoring, and use EventBridge rules for discrete state-change or system events.
Your answer is incorrect
Use the Lambda console to configure a trigger that invokes the Lambda function with CodePipeline as the event source

Explanation

Incorrect. The Lambda console does not let you configure a trigger that uses CodePipeline as the event source. Lambda triggers are set up from the event-producing service, such as Amazon S3 or Amazon DynamoDB Streams, or through Amazon EventBridge. CodePipeline does not support this direct trigger configuration from the Lambda console. Keyword tip: if an option describes configuring a Lambda trigger directly from the Lambda console for a service that does not natively support that integration, treat it as a likely distractor.
Use the CodePipeline console to set up a trigger for the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. The CodePipeline console does not provide a built-in feature to configure a trigger for a Lambda function. This integration must be configured through an Amazon EventBridge rule that uses CodePipeline as the event source. Keyword tip: watch for options that claim a source service's own console can directly wire up a Lambda trigger, when the real integration path is through EventBridge.

This question tests knowledge of how to connect AWS CodePipeline to AWS Lambda for event-driven notifications on pipeline state changes. Amazon EventBridge is the correct mechanism because it delivers a near real-time stream of system events that describe changes in AWS resources, and it lets you create rules that match specific events and route them to one or more targets, such as a Lambda function. CloudWatch alarms only monitor metric thresholds, not discrete state-change events, and neither the Lambda console nor the CodePipeline console natively supports configuring this type of cross-service trigger. When a scenario describes reacting to a state or status change in one AWS service by invoking another service like Lambda, an EventBridge rule is the default architectural choice.

Consider this scenario: Truenorth Systems runs frequent software updates to ground station control systems through CodePipeline, and the operations team needs immediate Slack or email alerts whenever a deployment stage fails or succeeds, since delays in detecting a failed deployment could disrupt satellite communication uptime. By creating an EventBridge rule that watches CodePipeline state changes and targets a Lambda function, the team gets automatic, near real-time notifications without polling or manual monitoring.

Question 23Incorrect

Wintergreen Bureau's mobile app lets subscribers view usage details after signing in via SAML federation. A new feature delivers notifications and offers to app users who are not required to log in.

What is the MOST efficient method to grant these unauthenticated users access to AWS resources?

Your answer is incorrect
Use Amazon Cognito Federated Identities and set up authentication using a Cognito User Pool

Explanation

Incorrect. A Cognito User Pool provides authenticated access. Users must sign up or sign in with credentials to use a User Pool. This scenario states that users will not log in, so a User Pool authentication flow adds unnecessary complexity. Keyword tip: any mention of a Cognito User Pool signals authenticated access, not anonymous access.
Embed access keys in the application that have limited access to resources

Explanation

Incorrect. Embedding long-term access keys inside a mobile application is a security anti-pattern. Attackers can extract the keys from the compiled application package. AWS best practice is to issue temporary, scoped credentials through a managed service instead of hardcoding keys. Keyword tip: any option that embeds or hardcodes access keys in client-side code is always wrong.
Correct answer
Use Amazon Cognito to associate unauthenticated users with an IAM role that has limited access to resources

Explanation

Correct. Amazon Cognito Identity Pools support unauthenticated, or guest, identities. Cognito Identity Pools issue a unique identity and temporary AWS credentials to users who never sign in. These temporary credentials map to an IAM role that grants only the minimal permissions needed, such as read-only access to a notifications resource. This approach is efficient to set up and secure, because no long-term credentials are exposed. Keyword tip: the phrase "unauthenticated identities" or "guest access" combined with Cognito Identity Pools always points to this pattern.
Use an IAM SAML 2.0 identity provider to establish trust

Explanation

Incorrect. An IAM SAML 2.0 identity provider federates access for users who already authenticated against an external identity source, such as a corporate directory. In this scenario, users do not log in at all, so there is no external identity assertion to trust. SAML federation requires an existing authenticated identity, which does not fit an anonymous access scenario. Keyword tip: SAML 2.0 identity providers signal that users already have a corporate or external login, not anonymous access.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon Cognito Identity Pools and their ability to grant temporary, scoped AWS credentials to unauthenticated users without any sign-in flow. Use a Cognito User Pool or a SAML 2.0 identity provider when users must authenticate through an identity source first. Use an unauthenticated Identity Pool role when the application must support anonymous access to a limited set of AWS resources. The decision logic depends on recognizing that hardcoded credentials violate security best practices, while Cognito's built-in unauthenticated role mapping provides temporary, least-privilege access with minimal setup effort.

A similar situation: Wintergreen Bureau wants app users to receive promotional offers immediately after installing the app, without creating an account first. By configuring an unauthenticated Cognito Identity Pool role scoped to read-only access on the notifications data source, Wintergreen Bureau lets every installed app instance retrieve offers securely, without exposing long-term credentials or forcing subscribers through a login screen.

Question 24Correct

A Team Lead at Greystone Enterprises deploys code to Amazon EC2 instances using AWS CodeCommit and AWS CodeDeploy. The deployment process must change permissions on deployed files and verify that the deployment succeeded. Which action should the Team Lead take?

Define an appspec.yml file in the codebuild/ directory

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeDeploy requires the AppSpec file to be placed in the root directory of the application's source code. AWS CodeDeploy does not look inside a codebuild/ subdirectory for this file. If AWS CodeDeploy cannot find appspec.yml in the root directory, the deployment fails. Keyword tip: if you see 'appspec.yml' paired with any location other than the root directory, treat that option as incorrect.
Define a buildspec.yml file in the root directory

Explanation

Incorrect. A buildspec.yml file belongs to AWS CodeBuild. AWS CodeBuild uses this file to specify build commands and settings for compiling and packaging source code. This file does not manage file permissions and does not validate an AWS CodeDeploy deployment. Keyword tip: associate 'buildspec.yml' only with AWS CodeBuild build phases, never with AWS CodeDeploy permission settings or validation hooks.
Define a buildspec.yml file in the codebuild/ directory

Explanation

Incorrect. A buildspec.yml file belongs to AWS CodeBuild. AWS CodeBuild uses this file to define build commands and build phases. AWS CodeDeploy does not use buildspec.yml to manage file permissions or to verify deployment success. Keyword tip: 'buildspec.yml' always points to AWS CodeBuild, not AWS CodeDeploy.
Your answer is correct
Define an appspec.yml file in the root directory

Explanation

Correct. AWS CodeDeploy requires a YAML-formatted file named appspec.yml. This file must be placed in the root directory of the application's source code structure. The AppSpec file maps source files to their destination locations on the instance, sets custom permissions for the deployed files, and defines lifecycle event hooks. These lifecycle hooks let AWS CodeDeploy run scripts at specific stages, such as validating that the deployment succeeded. Keyword tip: the combination of 'appspec.yml', 'root directory', 'permissions', and 'validate deployment' always identifies the AWS CodeDeploy AppSpec file.

AWS CodeDeploy requires an AppSpec file named appspec.yml, placed in the root directory of the application's source code revision. The AppSpec file maps source files to their destination locations, sets custom file permissions for those files, and defines lifecycle hooks such as ApplicationStart and ValidateService. These lifecycle hooks run scripts that confirm whether a deployment succeeded. A buildspec.yml file serves a completely different purpose: AWS CodeBuild uses it only to define build commands, and it has no role in managing permissions or validating deployments. When a scenario describes changing file permissions or validating deployment success on Amazon EC2 instances through AWS CodeDeploy, the correct artifact is always the appspec.yml file in the root directory.

Applied example: At Greystone Enterprises, the platform engineering team deploys updates to its social media analytics dashboard on Amazon EC2 instances several times per week. Each deployment package includes an appspec.yml file in the root directory that sets correct file permissions for the application's configuration files and runs a ValidateService hook to confirm the dashboard service starts correctly before AWS CodeDeploy marks the deployment as successful. This setup lets the newly promoted Team Lead catch failed deployments automatically instead of relying on manual checks.

Question 25Correct

At Larkspur Consolidated, EC2-hosted test infrastructure fails whenever the application tries to read firmware images from an Amazon S3 bucket. What should the company do to resolve this issue? (Select TWO.)

Check the security groups attached to the EC2 instances to ensure the required inbound rules are in place.

Explanation

Incorrect. Security groups control network traffic at the instance level. Inbound rules control traffic coming into the instance. The application in this scenario makes an outbound call to Amazon S3, so inbound rules do not affect this call. Keyword tip: when an EC2 instance calls out to another AWS service, check IAM permissions and bucket policies, not inbound security group rules.
Your selection is correct
Verify the IAM roles attached to the EC2 instances and ensure they have the necessary permissions to access the S3 bucket.

Explanation

Correct. An IAM role attached to an EC2 instance provides temporary credentials through an instance profile. The application uses these credentials to call AWS services such as Amazon S3. If the IAM role's policy does not include the required S3 actions, such as s3:GetObject or s3:PutObject, the application cannot access the bucket even if the bucket policy allows it. Keyword tip: IAM roles and instance profiles are the identity-side access control for EC2-to-S3 calls and are a primary checkpoint when troubleshooting access-denied errors.
Validate the VPC peering connections to ensure the S3 bucket is reachable.

Explanation

Incorrect. VPC peering connects two VPCs so private traffic can flow between them. Amazon S3 is a public AWS service, and instances reach it over the internet or through a VPC endpoint, not through VPC peering. Checking VPC peering connections would not help diagnose or fix this S3 access failure. Keyword tip: for private connectivity to S3 from inside a VPC, look for a VPC endpoint, not a VPC peering connection.
Modify the Amazon S3 bucket to be public to allow the EC2 instances to access it.

Explanation

Incorrect. Making the S3 bucket public would allow any unauthenticated user on the internet to access the bucket's contents. This action violates the principle of least privilege and creates a serious security risk. The correct fix is to grant the EC2 instance's IAM role scoped access through IAM policies and bucket policies, not to remove access controls. Keyword tip: making a resource public is almost never the correct answer in an access-denied troubleshooting question.
Your selection is correct
Check the bucket policies for the Amazon S3 bucket and confirm that they permit access from the EC2 instances.

Explanation

Correct. An Amazon S3 bucket policy is a resource-based policy. This policy defines which principals can access the bucket and which actions each principal can perform. If the bucket policy does not allow the EC2 instance's IAM role, the connection fails even when the IAM role itself has enough permissions. Keyword tip: bucket policies are the resource-side access control for S3 and must be checked alongside IAM role permissions.

This question tests the two independent access-control layers that govern EC2-to-S3 access: the IAM role attached to the EC2 instance, which is an identity-based policy, and the S3 bucket policy on the target bucket, which is a resource-based policy. Both layers must allow the required actions for the connection to succeed. A denial on either layer causes an access failure, so troubleshooting must check both layers instead of assuming only one is at fault. Security groups control network-level traffic and do not apply to this scenario, and VPC peering only applies to private connectivity between VPCs, not to public AWS services like S3.

In practice: Larkspur Consolidated's engineering team would first check the IAM role attached to the EC2 test instances for missing S3 permissions, then check the S3 bucket policy for the firmware-image bucket to confirm it allows access from that role. This two-step check quickly narrows down whether the block is on the identity side or the resource side, without ever needing to make the bucket public.

Question 26Correct

During a recent reliability audit, engineers found that failed Lambda invocations were being silently discarded, leaving no record for troubleshooting. A new member of the platform team at Foxglove International, a telecommunications provider, is now configuring a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for AWS Lambda functions.

As the team's Developer Associate, help the new team member identify the use cases in which AWS Lambda will add a message into a DLQ after processing an event. (Select TWO.)

The event has been processed successfully

Explanation

Incorrect. A successfully processed event is never sent to a dead-letter queue. The DLQ mechanism exists specifically to capture events that could not be processed. Keyword tip: associate DLQs with failure and expiration scenarios, not successful completions.
The Lambda function invocation failed only once but succeeded thereafter

Explanation

Incorrect. If an invocation fails once but a later retry succeeds, AWS Lambda treats the event as successfully processed. AWS Lambda does not send successfully processed events to the DLQ. Keyword tip: only events that fail all retry attempts qualify for the DLQ.
The Lambda function invocation is synchronous

Explanation

Incorrect. Synchronous invocations do not use dead-letter queues. The caller waits for an immediate response, so AWS Lambda returns any failure directly to the caller instead of queuing the event. Keyword tip: DLQs pair with decoupled, asynchronous patterns, not synchronous request/response calls.
Your selection is correct
The Lambda function invocation is asynchronous

Explanation

Correct. Dead-letter queues apply only to asynchronous invocations. When an asynchronous event exceeds its maximum age or exhausts all retry attempts, AWS Lambda discards the event or sends the event to the DLQ, if one is configured. Keyword tip: DLQ is an asynchronous-invocation feature only.
Your selection is correct
The event fails all processing attempts

Explanation

Correct. A dead-letter queue behaves like an on-failure destination. The DLQ captures events that exhaust all processing attempts or expire before being successfully processed. Keyword tip: the phrase "fails all attempts" or "expires" signals the DLQ delivery condition.

This question tests understanding of when AWS Lambda routes failed events to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). This feature applies only to asynchronous invocations. Use a DLQ, or the newer on-failure Lambda Destinations, to capture events that exhaust all retry attempts or exceed the maximum event age. This approach lets a team inspect and reprocess failed events later without blocking the original caller. Synchronous invocations return errors directly to the caller and never populate a DLQ, and events that eventually succeed, even after an initial failure, are also excluded from the DLQ. The decision logic depends on two factors: the invocation type (asynchronous or synchronous) and the final outcome (all attempts failed or expired, versus eventual success).

A similar situation: Foxglove International, a telecommunications provider, processes millions of asynchronous billing-event notifications through Lambda each day. By configuring a DLQ for these functions, the engineering team ensures that any event which fails after all retry attempts lands in a queue for manual review instead of disappearing silently. This setup lets the team resolve failed billing updates without affecting customers who are waiting on synchronous API responses elsewhere in the system.

Question 27Correct

Timberline Guild uses AWS CodeDeploy with an appspec.yml file to deploy an application from GitHub to Amazon EC2 instances running Amazon Linux. The company wants a final lifecycle event hook that verifies the deployment succeeded.

Which hook event should be used to verify the success of the deployment?

AfterInstall

Explanation

Incorrect. AfterInstall runs scripts for tasks such as configuring the application, setting file permissions, or performing other setup work after CodeDeploy copies the revision files to the instance. AfterInstall occurs well before CodeDeploy verifies that the deployment is fully complete. Keyword tip: associate AfterInstall with post-copy configuration tasks, not final validation.
ApplicationStart

Explanation

Incorrect. ApplicationStart runs scripts that restart services or processes that stopped during the ApplicationStop event. ApplicationStart does not validate whether the deployment succeeded. Keyword tip: associate ApplicationStart with restarting the application, not with final verification.
AllowTraffic

Explanation

Incorrect. AllowTraffic is a lifecycle event that the CodeDeploy agent uses to re-enable traffic to instances behind a load balancer after a deployment. AllowTraffic does not run custom validation scripts. Keyword tip: AllowTraffic is agent-controlled and not scriptable, so it cannot serve as a custom validation hook.
Your answer is correct
ValidateService

Explanation

Correct. ValidateService is the last lifecycle event in the standard EC2/On-Premises deployment sequence. AWS CodeDeploy runs ValidateService to execute scripts that check whether the deployment succeeded, such as smoke tests or health checks. Keyword tip: when a question asks about confirming or validating a deployment's success as the final step, think ValidateService.

AWS CodeDeploy runs a fixed sequence of lifecycle events for EC2/On-Premises deployments, and each event exists for a specific purpose. BeforeInstall and AfterInstall handle configuration tasks before and after CodeDeploy copies the application files to the instance. ApplicationStart and ApplicationStop start and stop the application, and AllowTraffic and BlockTraffic control load balancer traffic during the deployment. ValidateService runs last and is the correct place to add custom verification scripts, such as health checks, because CodeDeploy does not mark the deployment as successful until ValidateService completes without error.

Real-world example: Timberline Guild can add a smoke-test script to the ValidateService hook that calls a health-check endpoint on the newly deployed claims-processing application and confirms that the endpoint returns a successful response before CodeDeploy marks the deployment as complete. This approach lets the insurance company catch broken deployments automatically, instead of relying on manual verification after each release.

Question 28Correct

Fernbrook Solutions' mobile app lets customers redeem virtual credits for accessories. Each redemption must update the CustomerCredits and AccessoryInventory DynamoDB tables as an all-or-nothing operation: either both succeed or neither is applied. As a developer, how should you implement this?

Capture the transactions in the CustomerCredits table using DynamoDB Streams and then sync with the AccessoryInventory table

Explanation

Incorrect. DynamoDB Streams records a time-ordered sequence of item-level changes only after those changes have already been committed. DynamoDB Streams is a change-data-capture tool, not a transactional coordination tool. DynamoDB Streams cannot guarantee that an update to one table and an update to another table either both succeed or both fail together. Keyword tip: when a question pairs 'Streams' with 'sync tables,' recognize this as an asynchronous, eventually-consistent pattern that cannot enforce atomicity.
Use the BatchWriteItem API to update multiple tables simultaneously

Explanation

Incorrect. BatchWriteItem can write to multiple tables in a single call, but BatchWriteItem does not guarantee atomicity. Some write operations in the batch can succeed while other write operations fail, and DynamoDB returns the failed items separately so the application can retry them. Keyword tip: 'Batch' operations in DynamoDB exist for throughput efficiency, not for transactional guarantees; if a question mentions 'atomic' or 'all-or-nothing,' rule out BatchWriteItem and BatchGetItem.
Your answer is correct
Use the TransactWriteItems API of DynamoDB Transactions

Explanation

Correct. The TransactWriteItems API groups up to 25 write actions across one or more DynamoDB tables, within the same AWS account and Region, into a single synchronous, all-or-nothing operation. This guarantees that the CustomerCredits table and the AccessoryInventory table are updated together, or neither table is updated at all. Keyword tip: when a scenario requires atomic, all-or-nothing writes across multiple items or tables in DynamoDB, look for the phrases 'DynamoDB Transactions' or 'TransactWriteItems.'
Capture the transactions in the AccessoryInventory table using DynamoDB Streams and then sync with the CustomerCredits table

Explanation

Incorrect. This option relies on DynamoDB Streams to propagate changes after the fact, the same as option 1. This approach produces asynchronous, eventually-consistent syncing between tables, not an atomic, simultaneous update. Keyword tip: DynamoDB Streams exists to react to changes, for example by triggering a Lambda function, not to enforce transactional consistency between tables.

This question tests the difference between DynamoDB Transactions and other multi-item or multi-table operations, such as BatchWriteItem and DynamoDB Streams. Use TransactWriteItems, or TransactGetItems for reads, whenever a requirement calls for atomic, all-or-nothing updates across up to 25 actions spanning multiple items or tables within the same AWS account and Region; an optional client token can also be added for idempotency. Use BatchWriteItem when efficient bulk writes are needed but atomicity is not required, since partial failures are possible and the application must handle retries. Use DynamoDB Streams when the application needs to react to changes after they are committed, for example for auditing, replication, or triggering downstream processing, but never rely on DynamoDB Streams to enforce transactional consistency between tables.

A similar situation: an IoT device manufacturer like Fernbrook Solutions runs a customer loyalty program where credits are earned in one table and redeemed against inventory in another table. If the credit deduction and the inventory update are not linked by an atomic transaction, a system failure between the two writes could let a customer redeem credits without the inventory ever being decremented, or the reverse. Using TransactWriteItems ensures both tables always move together, keeping the loyalty program's data consistent even during partial system failures.

Question 29Correct

Birchwood Institute uses a BGP-enabled AWS Site-to-Site VPN to connect on-premises call-routing servers to EC2 instances hosting media relay services. Traffic reaches an EC2 instance in Subnet-X, but not one in Subnet-Y, though both subnets are in the same VPC.

Which logging mechanism should the team use to confirm whether traffic is reaching Subnet-Y?

Consult AWS Config logs to trace the traffic.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Config tracks and records changes to the configuration of AWS resources over time, and it evaluates those configurations against compliance rules. AWS Config has no visibility into live network traffic flow. Keyword tip: treat AWS Config as a configuration-history and compliance tool, not a network traffic diagnostic tool.
Check Amazon CloudWatch Logs for the EC2 instance in Subnet-Y.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudWatch Logs for an EC2 instance typically capture operating system logs, application logs, or agent-generated log data. Amazon CloudWatch Logs do not capture network-level packet flow information between subnets unless VPC Flow Logs are separately configured to publish into CloudWatch Logs. Keyword tip: standard CloudWatch Logs from an instance do not show inbound or outbound IP traffic at the interface level on their own.
Your answer is correct
Use VPC Flow Logs to check the inbound and outbound traffic of Subnet-Y.

Explanation

Correct. VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic moving to and from network interfaces inside a VPC. VPC Flow Logs record both accepted and rejected traffic at the subnet, network interface, or VPC level. This lets the team confirm whether packets destined for Subnet-Y are actually arriving, and whether those packets are being accepted or rejected because of a misconfigured route table, security group, or network ACL. Keyword tip: when a question asks how to confirm or troubleshoot actual network traffic reachability at the IP level inside a VPC, VPC Flow Logs is the correct tool.
Use AWS CloudTrail logs to verify traffic to Subnet-Y.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CloudTrail records API calls made against AWS services. AWS CloudTrail does not record the actual IP packet flow at the network interface level. The team needs to see whether packets reach Subnet-Y, not whether someone called an API. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks about verifying network traffic reachability between subnets, treat CloudTrail as a distractor, because CloudTrail is an API-activity audit tool, not a packet-level diagnostic tool.

This question tests the ability to choose the correct AWS logging service for diagnosing network reachability problems inside a VPC. VPC Flow Logs are purpose-built to record accepted and rejected IP traffic at the network interface, subnet, or VPC level, which makes VPC Flow Logs the correct tool whenever a scenario involves confirming whether traffic actually reaches a specific resource. AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, and standard Amazon CloudWatch Logs each serve a different purpose: AWS CloudTrail records API calls, AWS Config records configuration changes and compliance state, and standard CloudWatch Logs record operating system or application output. None of these three alternatives show live packet-level traffic, so none of them can confirm whether traffic reached Subnet-Y.

Business scenario: Birchwood Institute's media relay servers sit in Subnet-Y, and dropped internal calls are directly affecting the video conferencing experience customers pay for. By enabling VPC Flow Logs on Subnet-Y, the infrastructure team can see whether traffic from the on-premises call-routing servers is arriving and being accepted, or being rejected by a security group or network ACL rule, allowing the team to pinpoint the exact cause of the dropped connections quickly.

Question 30Correct

Vertex National, a cruise line operator that manages passenger data across its fleet's booking systems, needs to store sensitive customer records in Amazon S3 with encryption at rest enforced. The security team requires that the encryption keys be rotated no less than once per year.

What is the easiest way to implement a solution for this requirement?

Your answer is correct
Use AWS KMS with automatic key rotation

Explanation

Correct. SSE-KMS lets AWS manage the encryption key inside AWS KMS. When the key is a customer managed key generated inside AWS KMS, automatic key rotation can be turned on with one setting. AWS KMS then rotates the key material every year without any extra code or manual steps. Keyword tip: look for "SSE-KMS" combined with "automatic key rotation" as the simplest built-in rotation option.
Use SSE-C with automatic key rotation on an annual basis

Explanation

Incorrect. With SSE-C, the customer supplies the encryption key for each request. Amazon S3 performs the encryption and decryption, but Amazon S3 does not store the key or rotate it automatically. The customer must manage and rotate the key manually. Keyword tip: SSE-C means the customer supplies and rotates the key manually.
Encrypt the data before sending it to Amazon S3

Explanation

Incorrect. Encrypting data before sending it to Amazon S3 is called client-side encryption. In this approach, the customer application generates, stores, and rotates the encryption key. Amazon S3 never sees the unencrypted data or manages the key lifecycle. Keyword tip: client-side encryption always means the customer owns the entire key lifecycle.
Import a custom key into AWS KMS and automate the key rotation on an annual basis by using a Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS KMS does not support automatic rotation for imported key material. A custom Lambda function could rotate an imported key, but building and maintaining that function adds operational work. This extra work is unnecessary when a customer managed key created inside AWS KMS already supports automatic rotation. Keyword tip: imported key material in AWS KMS always disables automatic rotation.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon S3 encryption options and which option gives the simplest automatic key rotation. SSE-KMS with a customer managed key is the best choice when annual key rotation is required, because AWS KMS rotates the key material automatically once per year with no extra setup. SSE-C, client-side encryption, and imported key material all require the customer to manage and rotate the key manually. The decision logic is simple: choose the option that shifts key rotation responsibility to AWS instead of leaving it with the customer.

Practical example: Vertex National could store passenger payment records and loyalty program data in an Amazon S3 bucket protected with SSE-KMS. By turning on automatic key rotation for the customer managed key, the security team meets its annual rotation requirement without writing extra rotation code or tracking rotation dates manually.

Question 31Correct

The data protection team at Keystone Trust, an agricultural cooperative headquartered in Des Moines, Iowa, must encrypt a large volume of sensitive member financial records before the records are archived. A developer on the team will use an existing AWS KMS customer master key (CMK), named keystone-trust-financial-cmk, to produce the data encryption key.

The current key policy attached to keystone-trust-financial-cmk looks like this:

  1. {
  2.   "Sid": "Allow Key Usage",
  3.   "Effect": "Allow",
  4.   "Principal": {
  5.     "AWS": [
  6.       "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/KeystoneTrustCMKUser"
  7.     ]
  8.   },
  9.   "Action": [
  10.     "kms:Encrypt",
  11.     "kms:Decrypt",
  12.     "kms:ReEncrypt*",
  13.     "kms:DescribeKey"
  14.   ],
  15.   "Resource": "*"
  16. }


What additional API action must be added to the key policy to support this use case?

kms:CreateKey

Explanation

Incorrect. The kms:CreateKey action creates a brand-new customer master key (CMK) in the AWS account and region. In this scenario, the CMK named keystone-trust-financial-cmk already exists. The team needs permission to generate a data encryption key for encrypting a large volume of records, not permission to create a new CMK. Keyword tip: kms:CreateKey appears in scenarios about provisioning a new key, not about using an existing key for bulk data encryption.
kms:GetKeyPolicy

Explanation

Incorrect. The kms:GetKeyPolicy action only allows a user to retrieve the JSON key policy document attached to a CMK. This action has no connection to encryption operations or data key generation. Keyword tip: any "Get*" or "Describe*" KMS action relates to reading metadata about a key, not to performing cryptographic operations with that key.
kms:EnableKey

Explanation

Incorrect. The kms:EnableKey action sets the state of a CMK to "enabled." This action controls whether the CMK can be used at all for any cryptographic operation. This action does not grant permission to generate a data encryption key. Keyword tip: enable and disable actions manage the operational state of a CMK, not the specific operations a principal can perform with that CMK.
Your answer is correct
kms:GenerateDataKey

Explanation

Correct. A CMK can directly encrypt only up to 4 KB of data. To encrypt a large volume of sensitive records, an application must use the envelope encryption pattern. In this pattern, the application calls kms:GenerateDataKey to receive a plaintext data encryption key and an encrypted copy of that same key. The application uses the plaintext data encryption key to encrypt the records locally, then deletes the plaintext key from memory and stores the encrypted copy of the key alongside the encrypted records. Keyword tip: whenever a question describes encrypting data larger than 4 KB or describes envelope encryption, kms:GenerateDataKey is the permission that must be present in the key policy.

This question tests understanding of AWS KMS key policies and the envelope encryption pattern used to encrypt large volumes of data. A CMK can encrypt only up to 4 KB of data directly. Because of this limit, an application must call kms:GenerateDataKey to obtain a data encryption key. The application uses this data encryption key locally to encrypt the actual records, and it stores the encrypted copy of that key alongside the encrypted records for later decryption with kms:Decrypt. Actions such as kms:CreateKey, kms:GetKeyPolicy, and kms:EnableKey serve different administrative purposes and do not support a bulk data encryption workflow, so a key policy missing kms:GenerateDataKey will block the envelope encryption process even if encrypt and decrypt permissions are already present.

Real-world example: Keystone Trust processes harvest transaction records and member financial data that must stay encrypted at rest. Instead of sending each full record to AWS KMS for direct encryption, the cooperative's application generates a unique data encryption key through kms:GenerateDataKey for each batch of records, encrypts the batch locally with that key, and stores only the small encrypted copy of the data encryption key next to the encrypted batch. This approach lets Keystone Trust encrypt large archives efficiently while keeping the CMK's cryptographic operations fast and within AWS KMS request limits.

Question 32Correct

Silverlake Authority manages a CloudFormation stack for its student assessment platform. Before rolling out an update, a developer wants to view a summary of the proposed changes without implementing them in production. How can the developer accomplish this?

Use a direct update

Explanation

Incorrect. A direct update applies changes to the live stack resources immediately. A direct update does not give the developer a chance to preview the impact first. This approach does not meet the requirement of reviewing changes before implementation. Keyword tip: the phrase "direct update" signals immediate execution, which is the opposite of a safe preview mechanism.
Use drift detection

Explanation

Incorrect. Drift detection identifies when the actual configuration of stack resources differs from the configuration defined in the CloudFormation template. Drift detection does not preview the effect of new proposed changes. Drift detection only reports on changes that already happened outside of CloudFormation. Keyword tip: associate the word "drift" with detecting unmanaged or out-of-band changes, not with previewing upcoming updates.
Create a StackSet

Explanation

Incorrect. A StackSet creates, updates, or deletes stacks across multiple AWS accounts and AWS Regions with a single operation. A StackSet addresses multi-account and multi-Region deployment. A StackSet does not preview changes to a single stack. Keyword tip: the term "StackSet" signals multi-account or multi-Region orchestration, not change previewing.
Your answer is correct
Create a Change Set

Explanation

Correct. A Change Set creates a preview of how proposed changes to a CloudFormation template or its parameters will affect the running resources in a stack. AWS CloudFormation does not apply these changes automatically. AWS CloudFormation only applies the changes when the developer explicitly executes the Change Set. This gives the developer a chance to review and validate the changes before they affect production resources. Keyword tip: when a question asks about previewing or reviewing stack changes before applying them, think "Change Set".

This question tests knowledge of AWS CloudFormation stack update mechanisms. A Change Set lets a developer preview the impact of proposed changes before applying them to live resources, so a developer should use a Change Set whenever a safe, reviewable way to validate updates is needed before execution. A direct update applies changes immediately, drift detection only identifies configuration deviations that already occurred outside of CloudFormation, and a StackSet manages stack deployments across multiple AWS accounts and Regions rather than previewing changes to a single stack. The core decision logic is to separate "preview before execution" (Change Set) from "immediate execution" (direct update), "deviation detection" (drift detection), and "multi-account or multi-Region orchestration" (StackSet).

Real-world example: Silverlake Authority's platform engineering team wants to update the CloudFormation stack that manages the compute resources for its student assessment platform. Before applying the update, the team creates a Change Set to confirm that the update will not unintentionally replace or delete a database resource that stores active student exam data. Only after reviewing the Change Set output does the team execute it, minimizing the risk of an unexpected outage during a school testing period.

Driftwood Dynamics needs its CI/CD pipeline to automatically deploy software packages to both Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual servers at its regional offices.

Which AWS service should the developer use to accomplish this task?

AWS Elastic Beanstalk

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a platform-as-a-service offering. Elastic Beanstalk deploys and scales web applications on AWS-managed infrastructure, such as Apache, Nginx, or IIS environments. Elastic Beanstalk does not support deployment to on-premises virtual servers. Keyword tip: Elastic Beanstalk only manages AWS-hosted application environments, not hybrid on-premises deployments.
Your answer is correct
AWS CodeDeploy

Explanation

Correct. AWS CodeDeploy automates software deployments to many compute targets. These targets include Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda, and on-premises servers. Driftwood Dynamics needs to deploy to both Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises virtual servers. CodeDeploy supports this hybrid deployment target list directly. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions deployment to a hybrid environment that includes both cloud instances and on-premises servers, choose CodeDeploy.
AWS CodeBuild

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeBuild is a continuous integration service. CodeBuild compiles source code, runs automated tests, and produces deployable software packages. CodeBuild does not deploy those packages to target instances or servers. Keyword tip: CodeBuild builds and tests code; CodeBuild does not perform deployment.
AWS CodePipeline

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodePipeline is a continuous delivery orchestration service. CodePipeline manages the build, test, and deploy phases of a release workflow. CodePipeline relies on other services, such as CodeBuild and CodeDeploy, to actually perform those phases. Keyword tip: CodePipeline orchestrates the release workflow; CodeDeploy performs the actual deployment work inside that workflow.

This question tests knowledge of how AWS Developer Tools divide responsibility across the CI/CD lifecycle. CodeBuild handles continuous integration by compiling code and running tests. CodeDeploy handles automated deployment to Amazon EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda, and on-premises servers. CodePipeline orchestrates the end-to-end release pipeline by coordinating other services. Elastic Beanstalk provides a managed platform for deploying and scaling web applications, but only within AWS-managed infrastructure. When a scenario requires deploying software packages to a mix of cloud-based and on-premises compute resources, choose CodeDeploy, because CodeDeploy is the only service among these four options built to target both environments directly.

Business scenario: Driftwood Dynamics, a construction and engineering firm, operates regional offices where some servers still run on-premises due to existing hardware investments, while other workloads have already moved to Amazon EC2. The development team wants one deployment mechanism that pushes the same application package to both environments without maintaining two separate deployment processes. AWS CodeDeploy meets this need directly, since CodeDeploy supports both Amazon EC2 instances and on-premises servers as deployment targets from a single service.

Question 34Correct

Kingsford Group streams sensor telemetry into an Amazon Kinesis data stream. An EC2 consumer instance reads from the stream only once every 48 hours and writes results to Amazon Redshift. Monitoring confirms sensors transmit correctly and the instance is healthy, yet much of the data is missing each run.

What is the MOST likely explanation?

The EC2 instance is failing intermittently

Explanation

Incorrect. The scenario states that monitoring logs confirm the EC2 instance is healthy. An intermittent instance failure would normally show up in those logs as errors or restarts. Keyword tip: do not select an instance-failure answer when the question explicitly confirms the instance is healthy.
Your answer is correct
Records are retained for 24 hours in the Kinesis data stream by default

Explanation

Correct. By default, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams keeps each record available for 24 hours. The consumer EC2 instance in this scenario only reads from the stream every 48 hours. This means every second batch of records expires and is deleted before the consumer instance can read it, which causes the missing data. Keyword tip: whenever a consumer's polling interval is longer than the stream's retention period, expect data loss. The default retention period is 24 hours, and it can be extended up to 8760 hours using the IncreaseStreamRetentionPeriod operation.
Amazon Redshift is not suitable for storing streaming data

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Redshift is a standard destination for storing processed streaming data after it leaves Kinesis. The data loss in this scenario happens before Redshift is ever involved, while records are still sitting in the Kinesis stream. Keyword tip: when a question describes data loss upstream of the storage step, do not blame the final storage service.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams has too many shards provisioned

Explanation

Incorrect. Shard count controls the read and write throughput capacity of a Kinesis data stream. Adding more shards does not change how long records stay in the stream. Because retention is unaffected, too many shards cannot explain missing data. Keyword tip: treat shard count as a throughput setting, not a retention setting.

This question tests the relationship between a Kinesis data stream's retention period and a consumer's polling interval. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stores each record for a default period of 24 hours, after which the record is permanently deleted from the stream. This retention period can be increased up to 8760 hours with the IncreaseStreamRetentionPeriod operation, decreased back down to a minimum of 24 hours with DecreaseStreamRetentionPeriod, and checked at any time with DescribeStream. A consumer must read data more frequently than the stream's retention period, or records will expire before they are ever processed; this rule matters regardless of shard count, downstream storage choice, or consumer health, since none of those factors affect how long a record survives inside the stream.

Applied example: Kingsford Group streams production-line sensor telemetry into Kinesis but only runs its EC2 consumer every 48 hours. Because the default retention period is 24 hours, every record older than 24 hours is deleted before the consumer's next run, so roughly half of each batch is lost. Kingsford Group can fix this by either running the consumer more often than every 24 hours or by using IncreaseStreamRetentionPeriod to extend the stream's retention window past 48 hours.

Question 35Incorrect

Brackenridge Holdings uses the AWS SDK for Java to run Scan operations against a 30 GB DynamoDB table storing session records. No indexes can be created to retrieve the required rows predictably, but the team wants to retrieve them as fast as possible. Which option improves the Scan operation's performance?

Use a Query

Explanation

Incorrect. A Query operation is far more efficient than a Scan because it uses the primary key, or an index, to retrieve items directly. A Query requires a partition key, and optionally a sort key condition or a Global or Local Secondary Index, to work. The scenario states that no index can be created to retrieve these items predictably. Because of this constraint, a Query cannot be used here. Keyword tip: Query needs a key schema or index; when indexing is ruled out in the scenario, Query is not a viable option.
Use a ProjectionExpression

Explanation

Incorrect. A ProjectionExpression only limits which attributes DynamoDB returns for each item that the Scan has already read. It reduces the size of the response payload, but it does not reduce the number of items DynamoDB must read. It also does not reduce the read capacity consumed. Because of this, a ProjectionExpression does not meaningfully speed up locating the target rows. Keyword tip: ProjectionExpression controls which columns come back, not which rows are read or how fast the scan finishes.
Your answer is incorrect
Use a FilterExpression

Explanation

Incorrect. A FilterExpression is applied only after DynamoDB has already read every item in the scanned segment and already consumed the read capacity for those items. A FilterExpression simply discards non-matching items from the result set before returning it to the application. It does not reduce the amount of data scanned, and it does not reduce cost or latency. Because of this, a FilterExpression does not improve Scan performance. Keyword tip: FilterExpression narrows results after the fact; it never reduces read capacity consumption or scan time.
Correct answer
Use parallel scans

Explanation

Correct. By default, a Scan operation reads a table's data sequentially in bounded pages, each capped at a fixed size of 1 megabyte. This becomes slow as the table grows larger. DynamoDB lets a Scan logically divide a table or secondary index into multiple segments. Multiple worker threads or processes can then scan these segments at the same time. This parallel approach significantly reduces the total time needed to retrieve all matching items. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions speeding up a full-table Scan with no index available, think "parallel Scan with multiple worker segments."

This question tests understanding of how to optimize Amazon DynamoDB Scan performance when a Query is not an option because no suitable key schema or index exists. A Scan operation reads data sequentially by default, which makes it slow and costly on large tables. Neither ProjectionExpression, which only limits returned attributes, nor FilterExpression, which only discards items after DynamoDB has already read them, reduces the underlying read cost or duration. Parallel scans solve this by logically dividing the table into segments that multiple worker threads or processes can scan at the same time, which directly reduces the wall-clock time needed to retrieve matching items; the decision logic is simple: use Query whenever a key condition is available, and fall back to parallel Scan only when scanning a large table without an index is unavoidable.

Real-world example: Brackenridge Holdings stores viewer session records in a 30 GB DynamoDB table without a key schema that matches its reporting needs. To generate nightly viewership reports quickly, the engineering team configures a parallel Scan that splits the table into several segments and assigns each segment to a separate worker thread, cutting the report generation time significantly compared to a single sequential Scan.

Question 36Incorrect

Stonebridge Corporation, a biotechnology research lab, has entered into a three-year data-sharing agreement with a partner hospital network. Under the agreement, monthly snapshots of the shared clinical trial database must be preserved for the entire three-year period to satisfy audit requirements.

The engineering team discovers that the Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) automated backup feature enforces a maximum retention window that falls short of this multi-year requirement.

Which of the following solutions can help meet this requirement?

Correct answer
Create a cron expression in Amazon EventBridge Scheduler that triggers an AWS Lambda function, which in turn triggers the database snapshot

Explanation

Correct. Amazon RDS automated backups have a maximum retention period of 35 days. This retention period is too short for a three-year compliance requirement. A scheduled Amazon EventBridge Scheduler rule using a cron expression can invoke an AWS Lambda function every month. The AWS Lambda function creates a manual DB snapshot each time it runs. Manual snapshots persist independently of the automated backup retention limit until someone deletes them. Keyword tip: when a scenario requires backup retention beyond the automated backup limit, look for a scheduled Lambda function that creates manual snapshots.
Enable RDS automated backups

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon RDS automated backups support a retention period between 0 and 35 days. A three-year retention requirement exceeds this maximum by a wide margin. Automated backups alone cannot meet a multi-year compliance requirement. Keyword tip: automated backups have a hard 35-day retention ceiling, so any multi-year requirement needs manually triggered, persistent snapshots instead.
Your answer is incorrect
Enable RDS Read Replicas

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon RDS read replicas copy data from a source database to one or more replica instances. Read replicas exist to offload read traffic and improve read scalability. Read replicas do not extend backup retention or store historical snapshots. Keyword tip: read replicas signal read scaling and performance, not backup retention or compliance archiving.
Enable RDS Multi-AZ

Explanation

Incorrect. Multi-AZ deployments create a standby database replica in a different Availability Zone. The standby replica exists to support automatic failover during an infrastructure failure. Multi-AZ deployments do not change or extend the backup retention period. Keyword tip: Multi-AZ signals high availability and failover, not long-term backup storage.

This question tests the difference between Amazon RDS features that manage availability and performance, and the mechanism needed for long-term backup retention. Automated RDS backups support a retention window of at most 35 days, so they cannot satisfy a multi-year compliance mandate. Manual DB snapshots do not expire automatically; they remain until someone deletes them, so they are the correct building block for long retention periods. Read replicas and Multi-AZ deployments solve different problems: read replicas scale read traffic, and Multi-AZ provides automatic failover, but neither one manages backup retention. When a requirement exceeds the automated backup window, the correct pattern is a scheduled job, such as an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler rule invoking an AWS Lambda function, that creates manual snapshots on a recurring basis.

In practice: Stonebridge Corporation's compliance team needs monthly database snapshots preserved for the full three-year duration of its data-sharing agreement with a partner hospital network. Because Amazon RDS automated backups only retain data for up to 35 days, Stonebridge configures an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler rule with a monthly cron expression that invokes an AWS Lambda function. The AWS Lambda function creates a manual snapshot of the clinical trial database each month, and each snapshot remains available for the full three years required by the agreement.

Question 37Correct

Ashford Innovations must instrument its application code to capture more detailed X-Ray diagnostic data than the default request information. The added instrumentation will generate large trace volumes, so the team needs trace data indexed for efficient filtering. What should the development team do?

Configure the necessary X-Ray environment variables

Explanation

Incorrect. X-Ray environment variables control how the SDK communicates with the X-Ray daemon, such as setting the daemon address or enabling and disabling tracing. These variables configure SDK behavior. They do not create indexed or filterable custom data fields. Keyword tip: environment variables control SDK configuration, not data indexing.
Your answer is correct
Add annotations to the segment document

Explanation

Correct. Annotations are simple key-value pairs added to a segment or subsegment document. AWS X-Ray automatically indexes annotations, up to 50 per trace, so they can be used in filter expressions or with the GetTraceSummaries API. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions filtering, searching, or indexing custom trace data, annotations are the answer.
Add metadata to the segment document

Explanation

Incorrect. Metadata key-value pairs can store arbitrary data types, including objects and lists, and appear in the trace details. AWS X-Ray does not index metadata. Metadata cannot be used in filter expressions. Keyword tip: metadata is for storing extra context only, never for searching or filtering.
Install the required plugins for the appropriate AWS SDK

Explanation

Incorrect. Installing SDK plugins records information about the AWS resources running the application, such as Amazon EC2 instance or Amazon ECS container details. Plugins do not create searchable or filterable custom trace fields. Keyword tip: plugins relate to compute-resource metadata, not to indexed custom data.

This question tests the distinction between annotations and metadata in AWS X-Ray instrumentation. Annotations are indexed key-value pairs, limited to 50 per trace, and are designed for filtering and grouping traces through filter expressions or the GetTraceSummaries API. Metadata supports richer data structures, such as objects and lists, but AWS X-Ray does not index metadata, so metadata only provides contextual storage. Use annotations when a scenario requires filtering or searching large volumes of custom trace data, and use metadata when the goal is only to attach descriptive information without needing to search on it. SDK plugins and environment variables serve different purposes entirely: plugins capture resource metadata about the compute environment, and environment variables configure SDK behavior. Neither plugins nor environment variables provide any indexing capability.

A similar situation: Ashford Innovations processes thousands of incoming relief requests through a distributed application during a disaster response. The development team adds annotations that record the affected region and request priority to each trace segment. This lets the team quickly filter traces in the X-Ray console to isolate slow or failed requests coming from a specific disaster zone, speeding up troubleshooting during time-critical operations.

Question 38Incorrect

Lattice Foundation must pass more than 5 MB of sensitive client data to Java-based AWS Lambda functions, encrypting and decrypting it at runtime.

Which method meets this requirement?

Your answer is incorrect
Use AWS KMS direct encryption and store the data as a file

Explanation

Incorrect. The AWS KMS Encrypt API used for direct encryption has a hard limit of 4 KB per payload. This limit applies regardless of how the encrypted result is stored afterward. A payload of 5 MB exceeds this limit, so KMS direct encryption cannot be used here. Keyword tip: the phrase 'KMS direct encryption' signals the 4 KB ceiling, which immediately rules it out for larger payloads.
Correct answer
Use envelope encryption and reference the data as a file within the code

Explanation

Correct. Envelope encryption encrypts the data locally using a data encryption key. AWS KMS only protects that small data key, not the actual payload. This design allows the encrypted data to be much larger than 4 KB, including payloads over 5 MB. The encrypted output can be packaged as a file inside the Lambda deployment package and read by the function code at runtime. Keyword tip: when a payload exceeds the 4 KB AWS KMS direct-encryption limit, envelope encryption with the AWS Encryption SDK and file-based storage is the correct pattern to recognize.
Use AWS KMS encryption and store the data as an environment variable

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS KMS direct encryption supports payloads up to only 4 KB. AWS Lambda environment variables also have a total size limit of 4 KB. Neither limit can support the 5 MB payload described in this scenario, regardless of which encryption method is used. Keyword tip: environment variables work well for small configuration secrets, not for multi-megabyte encrypted data.
Use envelope encryption and store the data as an environment variable

Explanation

Incorrect. Envelope encryption can protect large amounts of data. However, storing the encrypted output in a Lambda environment variable is still limited by the 4 KB total size cap on environment variables. This limit makes environment variables unsuitable for data larger than 4 KB, even when envelope encryption is used correctly. Keyword tip: check the storage destination's size limit separately from the encryption method's size limit.

AWS KMS direct encryption (the Encrypt API) only accepts payloads up to 4 KB, and AWS Lambda environment variables share the same 4 KB total limit, so both are unsuitable whenever a payload grows beyond that size. Envelope encryption solves this by generating a local data encryption key, using it to encrypt the actual payload, and then having AWS KMS protect only that small key rather than the full payload. Because the payload itself never has to pass through KMS, its size can grow well beyond 4 KB, making envelope encryption the standard approach for encrypting large objects such as files, backups, or client records. The encrypted output is then stored as a file, either bundled with the deployment package or fetched from a service such as Amazon S3, and decrypted inside the function at runtime.

Real-world example: A law firm like Lattice Foundation might process large scanned case files or client contracts through Lambda functions, where each file can be several megabytes. Direct KMS encryption or environment variables would fail immediately due to the 4 KB limit, so the engineering team uses envelope encryption to protect this sensitive legal data efficiently while keeping the KMS key management overhead minimal.

Question 39Correct

At Kingsford Works, consumers of an Amazon SQS queue poll in short cycles, and calls frequently return no messages even though messages are available, driving up SQS API costs. How can a Developer optimize message retrieval and reduce this cost?

Call the SetQueueAttributes API with the maxReceiveCount set to 20

Explanation

Incorrect. The maxReceiveCount parameter is part of a redrive policy. A redrive policy defines how many times a message can be received before Amazon SQS moves the message to a dead-letter queue. This parameter does not affect polling behavior. This parameter does not affect the number of empty responses. Keyword tip: maxReceiveCount signals dead-letter queue configuration, not polling optimization.
Call the ReceiveMessage API with the VisibilityTimeout parameter set to 30

Explanation

Incorrect. VisibilityTimeout controls how long a received message stays invisible to other consumers. This setting prevents duplicate processing of the same message. VisibilityTimeout does not influence whether ReceiveMessage waits for messages to arrive. VisibilityTimeout does not reduce the frequency of empty responses. Keyword tip: VisibilityTimeout is about preventing duplicate processing, not reducing polling cost.
Call the SetQueueAttributes API with the DelaySeconds parameter set to 900

Explanation

Incorrect. DelaySeconds controls how long a newly sent message stays hidden from consumers before becoming available for the first time. This setting is part of delay queue behavior. DelaySeconds does not affect how consumers poll for existing messages. DelaySeconds does not reduce empty API responses. Keyword tip: DelaySeconds relates to message visibility at send time, not retrieval efficiency.
Your answer is correct
Call the ReceiveMessage API with the WaitTimeSeconds parameter set to 20

Explanation

Correct. Setting WaitTimeSeconds to a value greater than 0 on the ReceiveMessage call enables long polling. The maximum value for WaitTimeSeconds is 20 seconds. With long polling, Amazon SQS waits until a message becomes available or the timeout expires before sending a response, instead of immediately returning an empty response. This behavior removes unnecessary empty responses and reduces the number of API calls, which lowers cost. Keyword tip: WaitTimeSeconds on ReceiveMessage means long polling, which means fewer wasted API calls.

This question tests understanding of Amazon SQS polling strategies. Amazon SQS supports two polling modes: short polling and long polling. Short polling is the default mode, and it queries only a subset of SQS servers, so a ReceiveMessage call can return an empty response even when messages exist in the queue. This behavior increases the number of API calls needed to retrieve messages, which increases cost. Long polling, enabled by setting WaitTimeSeconds to a value greater than 0 on the ReceiveMessage call, waits for a message to become available or for the timeout to expire before responding, which eliminates empty responses caused by partial server queries. A Developer should use long polling when consumers poll frequently and cost efficiency matters, and should use short polling only when near-real-time responses are required regardless of empty results. Parameters like DelaySeconds, VisibilityTimeout, and maxReceiveCount address different concerns and do not affect polling efficiency.

A similar situation: Kingsford Works runs a course-content ingestion pipeline where consumers process uploaded video lessons from an SQS queue. During peak enrollment periods, the consumers poll the queue in short cycles, and many ReceiveMessage calls return empty because short polling checks only a subset of servers. By enabling long polling with WaitTimeSeconds set to 20, Kingsford Works reduces the number of empty responses and lowers its SQS API call costs while keeping message processing responsive.

Question 40Correct

Overlook Cooperative, an online gaming company, runs several AWS Lambda functions that support its real-time leaderboard and matchmaking analytics. Each function is invoked by a different AWS service, such as Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service, or Amazon EventBridge.

These functions share a common characteristic: they process heavy workloads such as big data analysis, large file processing, and statistical computations.

What should a developer do to improve the performance of these AWS Lambda functions without changing the application code?

Change the Lambda function runtime to use Golang

Explanation

Incorrect. Switching the runtime to Golang means rewriting the function in a different programming language and redeploying it. This action directly violates the requirement of not changing the application code. A runtime change also does not guarantee better performance for a compute-heavy workload if the memory and CPU allocation stay the same. Keyword tip: any option that requires a runtime or language change conflicts with a "without changing code" constraint.
Change the instance type for the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda is a fully managed, serverless compute service. It does not expose instance types to the developer. The concept of an instance type belongs to Amazon EC2, where a customer picks a virtual machine size. Lambda instead abstracts the underlying compute infrastructure completely. Keyword tip: if an option mentions "instance type" in a Lambda scenario, treat it as a distractor, because Lambda has no selectable instance types.
Increase the Lambda function timeout

Explanation

Incorrect. The timeout setting only controls how long AWS Lambda allows the function to keep running before it is stopped. The timeout setting does not increase CPU power or execution speed. Raising the timeout can prevent a long-running task from being cut off early, but it does not make the function run faster. Keyword tip: timeout controls maximum duration allowed, not processing speed.
Your answer is correct
Increase the RAM assigned to the Lambda function

Explanation

Correct. In AWS Lambda, the memory setting controls more than RAM. Memory allocation also determines the proportional amount of CPU power, network bandwidth, and other resources given to the function. A developer can set memory between 128 megabytes and 10,240 megabytes, in 1-megabyte increments. At 1,769 megabytes, a function receives the equivalent of one full vCPU. Raising the memory value increases available compute power for CPU-heavy workloads, and this change requires no code modification. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks how to improve Lambda performance "without changing code," the correct action is almost always to raise the memory allocation.

AWS Lambda ties memory and CPU power together in a single configurable setting, so the amount of RAM a developer assigns to a function directly controls the compute power available to it, up to one full vCPU at 1,769 megabytes of memory. For a compute-intensive workload, such as big data analysis, large file processing, or statistical computation, the correct way to improve performance without touching the code is to raise this memory allocation. Increasing the timeout only extends the execution window and adds no compute power, changing the runtime requires rewriting the code (violating the stated constraint), and instance types do not exist in Lambda's serverless execution model, since Lambda abstracts away the underlying servers entirely.

Consider this scenario: Overlook Cooperative's matchmaking analytics function occasionally times out or runs slowly during peak online play sessions when it must crunch large batches of player statistics pulled in through Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose. Instead of rewriting the function or changing its runtime, the development team raises its memory allocation in the Lambda console, which proportionally increases the CPU power available and lets the function finish the same workload faster, with zero code changes.
