Question 41Incorrect

Wintergreen Group uses Amazon CloudFront with origin failover (origin groups) to distribute driver training videos to depots nationwide. Which of the following statements are correct regarding the configuration of CloudFront with Origin Groups? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
CloudFront routes all incoming requests to the primary origin, even when a previous request failed over to the secondary origin

Explanation

Correct. CloudFront routes every new viewer request to the primary origin first. CloudFront does this regardless of whether an earlier request failed over to the secondary origin. CloudFront does not remember a previous failover event and does not switch permanently to the secondary origin. Each new request re-evaluates the primary origin's health based on the response the primary origin returns. Keyword tip: remember that CloudFront origin failover is evaluated per request, not sticky.
Your selection is correct
CloudFront fails over to the secondary origin only when the HTTP method of the viewer request is GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS

Explanation

Correct. CloudFront fails over to the secondary origin in an origin group only when the viewer request uses the HTTP method GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS. CloudFront does not fail over for other methods, such as POST or PUT, because those methods are not idempotent. Retrying a non-idempotent request against a different origin could cause unintended side effects, like duplicate data changes. Keyword tip: link the phrase "GET, HEAD, OPTIONS only" to CloudFront origin failover trigger conditions.
In the origin group of your distribution, all the origins are defined as primary for automatic failover in case an origin fails

Explanation

Incorrect. An origin group can have only one origin marked as primary. The remaining origin or origins act as secondary origins. CloudFront uses a secondary origin only when the primary origin fails to respond correctly. A valid origin group configuration requires at least two origins, with exactly one origin marked as primary. Keyword tip: an origin group always has exactly one primary origin and one or more secondary origins.
Your selection is incorrect
When there is a cache hit, CloudFront routes the request to the primary origin in the origin group

Explanation

Incorrect. A cache hit means CloudFront already stores the requested object at the edge location. CloudFront serves the object directly from the edge cache without contacting any origin, primary or secondary. CloudFront only contacts the primary origin when there is a cache miss, meaning the object is not already cached. Keyword tip: a cache hit means CloudFront serves content from the edge cache and does not send a request to any origin.
To set up origin failover, you must have a distribution with at least three origins

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudFront origin failover requires a minimum of two origins in the origin group, not three. You create the origin group with two origins and mark one origin as primary. CloudFront automatically routes requests to the secondary origin when the primary origin returns specific failure responses, such as certain HTTP status codes. Keyword tip: remember that two origins is the minimum requirement for CloudFront origin failover.

CloudFront origin groups provide high availability by routing requests to a secondary origin when the primary origin fails specific health checks, such as defined HTTP status codes. Failover only applies to GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests, because these methods are idempotent and safe to retry against a different origin. Each origin group requires at least two origins, with exactly one origin marked as primary; CloudFront re-evaluates the primary origin's health on every new request rather than remembering past failover events. Cache hits bypass origin routing entirely, since CloudFront serves cached content directly from the edge location without contacting any origin.

Business scenario: The platform engineering team at Wintergreen Group uses CloudFront origin failover to keep driver training videos available across the country, even if the primary content server experiences an outage during peak shipping season. By configuring a secondary origin, such as a backup Amazon S3 bucket, the team ensures depot staff can still access training content without manual intervention if the primary origin fails.

Question 42Correct

Brightwater Trust stores agent performance data in a DynamoDB table named brightwater-agent-scores, with attributes user_id (partition key), user_name, user_score, and user_rank. Agents authenticate via web identity federation and may update only their own user_name attribute.

Which condition block should be added to the IAM policy for the dynamodb:PutItem call to enforce this?

"Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "dynamodb:LeadingKeys": ["${www.amazon.com:user_name}"], "dynamodb:Attributes": ["user_id"] } }

Explanation

Incorrect. This condition sets dynamodb:LeadingKeys to ${www.amazon.com:user_name}. The dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key must always match the table's partition key attribute. The partition key attribute in this table is user_id, not user_name. This condition also sets dynamodb:Attributes to user_id. The requirement states that agents can only write the user_name attribute, so this condition does the opposite of what is needed. Keyword tip: dynamodb:LeadingKeys must reference the partition key attribute, and that value must come from the identity provider's unique user identifier, not from the field the policy intends to update.
"Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "dynamodb:LeadingKeys": ["${www.amazon.com:user_name}"], "dynamodb:Attributes": ["user_name", "user_id"] } }

Explanation

Incorrect. This condition sets dynamodb:LeadingKeys to ${www.amazon.com:user_name}. This value is wrong, because the table's partition key attribute is user_id, not user_name. This condition also sets dynamodb:Attributes to include both user_name and user_id. This list is too broad, because agents should only be allowed to write user_name. This condition combines two separate mistakes into one policy. Keyword tip: check the LeadingKeys value and the Attributes list separately, because a policy can fail on either one even when the other one looks correct.
Your answer is correct
"Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "dynamodb:LeadingKeys": ["${www.amazon.com:user_id}"], "dynamodb:Attributes": ["user_name"] } }

Explanation

Correct. This condition sets dynamodb:LeadingKeys to ${www.amazon.com:user_id}. This value is correct, because user_id is the table's partition key attribute, and the value comes from the federated identity's unique user token. This condition sets dynamodb:Attributes to user_name only. This list matches the requirement exactly, because agents are only allowed to update the user_name attribute. Keyword tip: for fine-grained DynamoDB access control with web identity federation, match dynamodb:LeadingKeys to the partition key tied to the identity token, and list only the allowed writable field in dynamodb:Attributes.
"Condition": { "ForAllValues:StringEquals": { "dynamodb:LeadingKeys": ["${www.amazon.com:user_id}"], "dynamodb:Attributes": ["user_name", "user_id"] } }

Explanation

Incorrect. This condition sets dynamodb:LeadingKeys to ${www.amazon.com:user_id}. This part is correct, because user_id is the table's partition key attribute. This condition sets dynamodb:Attributes to include both user_name and user_id. This list is too broad. The requirement states that agents can update only the user_name attribute, so allowing a write to user_id breaks the least-privilege requirement. Keyword tip: dynamodb:Attributes must list only the exact fields the policy allows the caller to write, never more than that.

This question tests fine-grained access control (FGAC) on Amazon DynamoDB when a web identity federation user calls dynamodb:PutItem directly. The dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key controls which partition key value the caller can access. This value must always match the table's actual partition key attribute, and it must come from the identity provider's unique user token, not from the attribute the policy is trying to protect. The dynamodb:Attributes condition key controls which specific attributes the caller can write. This list must include only the fields the business requirement allows, never more. A correct policy pairs the right LeadingKeys value with the narrowest possible Attributes list; getting either piece wrong breaks the security requirement even if the other piece is correct.

Use case: Brightwater Trust could apply this same pattern to let real estate agents log in through a federated identity provider and update only their own display name in a shared agent-performance table, while preventing any agent from modifying scores, rankings, or other agents' records. This approach removes the need for a backend service to broker every write, which reduces operational overhead for the firm's engineering team.

Question 43Correct

Birchwood Global pushes custom metrics from hundreds of microservices to Amazon CloudWatch. Some PutMetricData calls intermittently fail with HTTP 400: ThrottlingException, and no data point is recorded when this happens. What best practice should the engineer first attempt to resolve this issue?

Analyze the application and remove the API call

Explanation

Incorrect. Removing the API call does not fix the problem. Removing the call also removes metric data that the application needs for monitoring. The correct goal is to reduce the throttling rate, not to remove functionality. Keyword tip: an option that suggests deleting a feature to fix an error is rarely correct on the exam.
Use the AWS CLI to get the metrics

Explanation

Incorrect. Switching to the AWS CLI instead of a direct API call does not solve the problem. The AWS CLI sends requests to the same underlying CloudWatch API. Those requests count toward the same per-account, per-Region rate limit. Keyword tip: changing the client tool without changing the call pattern does not remove throttling.
Your answer is correct
Retry the call with exponential backoff

Explanation

Correct. When CloudWatch returns a ThrottlingException, the engineer should retry the call using exponential backoff with jitter. This retry pattern spreads retry attempts out over time. Spreading the attempts out lowers the chance of hitting the same rate limit again. Many AWS SDKs already implement this retry pattern by default. Keyword tip: the combination of 'ThrottlingException', 'HTTP 400', and 'retry' points to exponential backoff as the correct first response.
Contact AWS Support for a limit increase

Explanation

Incorrect. Contacting AWS Support for a limit increase is not the first step. The engineer should first apply best practices such as retrying with exponential backoff, spacing out API calls, and batching metrics into fewer calls. Requesting a higher limit can also increase the AWS bill. Keyword tip: a 'limit increase' is a last resort, not the first troubleshooting step, when a service returns a ThrottlingException.

This question tests knowledge of how to handle API throttling errors, such as HTTP 400: ThrottlingException, returned by AWS services like Amazon CloudWatch. The recommended best practice is to retry failed calls using exponential backoff with jitter, space calls out over time, and batch multiple metrics into fewer API calls. A Developer should consider more drastic steps only after applying these practices: requesting a service limit increase can raise costs, and removing functionality sacrifices observability. The correct decision logic is to always start with client-side retry and request-shaping strategies before escalating to AWS Support for a limit increase.

Consider this scenario: Birchwood Global ingests engagement metrics from hundreds of microservices into CloudWatch to power its real-time analytics dashboard. During traffic spikes, some PutMetricData calls exceed the per-account CloudWatch API rate limit and return ThrottlingException errors. Instead of requesting a limit increase right away, Birchwood Global's engineers implement exponential backoff with jitter in their metric-publishing code, which resolves most of the throttling without any additional cost or AWS Support ticket.

Question 44Correct

The platform engineering team at Truenorth Holdings, a regional airline, is building a REST service using Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda integration to support upcoming flight-scheduling features. The service must support running different versions of the API simultaneously for testing purposes.

What is the BEST way to accomplish this?

Use an X-Version header to denote which version is being called, and pass that header value to the Lambda function(s)

Explanation

Incorrect. API Gateway has no built-in mechanism that routes a request to a specific Lambda function version or alias based on a custom header value. The integration target, meaning the Lambda function, version, or alias, is configured statically per stage. The integration target is not inferred dynamically from a header at request time. Keyword tip: custom headers can carry application-level metadata, but custom headers cannot replace stage-based routing when the goal is switching backend integration targets.
Create an API Gateway Lambda authorizer to route API clients to the correct API version

Explanation

Incorrect. A Lambda authorizer performs custom authentication and authorization logic. A Lambda authorizer validates bearer tokens or request parameters before allowing a request to proceed. A Lambda authorizer is not designed to route requests to different API versions. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions validating a token or a custom authentication scheme, think Lambda authorizer; for version routing, think stages.
Create an API Gateway resource policy to isolate versions and provide context to the Lambda function(s)

Explanation

Incorrect. A resource policy controls which principals can invoke an API. Principals include accounts, VPCs, and IP ranges. A resource policy is an access-control mechanism. A resource policy does not isolate API versions and does not pass contextual configuration to a Lambda function. Keyword tip: if a scenario is about restricting network or account-based access, think resource policy; if a scenario is about versioning, think stages.
Your answer is correct
Deploy each API version as a unique stage with a unique endpoint, and use stage variables to provide further context

Explanation

Correct. A stage is a named reference to a deployment. A deployment is a snapshot of the API at a specific point in time. Each stage has its own unique invoke URL. Stage variables act like environment variables that you can reference in integration request settings, such as the Lambda function ARN or alias. Stage variables let different stages point to different backend versions. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions running multiple API versions or environments, such as dev, test, or prod, side by side, think of API Gateway stages combined with stage variables.

This question tests knowledge of how to manage multiple versions or environments of a REST API built with API Gateway and Lambda. A stage is an independent, named snapshot of an API, such as dev, test, v1, or v2, and each stage has its own invoke URL and its own settings for caching, throttling, and logging. Stage variables let you parameterize the integration, for example pointing to a different Lambda alias or ARN, without duplicating the API definition. A resource policy controls access based on the caller's identity or network location, not the API version, a Lambda authorizer controls authentication and authorization rather than version selection, and a custom header cannot change API Gateway's backend integration target at request time. When a scenario calls for running multiple API versions at the same time for testing, the correct approach is stages combined with stage variables.

Use case: Truenorth Holdings' platform engineering team could deploy a v1 stage for the current production flight-scheduling API and a separate v2 stage for a new fare-calculation feature under active testing. Each stage points to a different Lambda alias through a stage variable, so QA engineers can test the new version at its own dedicated endpoint without affecting live passenger-facing traffic. Once testing passes, the team promotes the v2 stage to production by updating the stage variable, with no changes required to the API definition itself.

Question 45Correct

Overlook Labs runs a fleet of Amazon ECS tasks for a Dockerized data-processing service that ingests real-time readings from laboratory instruments. To keep pace with sudden spikes in researcher activity, the platform team now needs the service to scale out based on user load within 15 seconds.

How should the developer instrument the application code so that this requirement can be met?

Create a standard-resolution custom Amazon CloudWatch metric for user activity data, then publish data every 30 seconds

Explanation

Incorrect. Standard-resolution metrics can only be retrieved with a 1-minute granularity. A 1-minute granularity is far too coarse to detect and react to load changes within a 15-second window. Keyword tip: any requirement for sub-minute detection or response rules out standard-resolution metrics entirely.
Create a standard-resolution custom Amazon CloudWatch metric for user activity data, then publish data every 5 seconds

Explanation

Incorrect. Standard-resolution custom metrics are always aggregated by CloudWatch to a 1-minute granularity, no matter how often the application publishes data points. Publishing every 5 seconds does not change this behavior, so the effective granularity remains too coarse for a 15-second detection window. Keyword tip: standard resolution always has a 60-second floor for granularity, regardless of publish frequency.
Create a high-resolution custom Amazon CloudWatch metric for user activity data, then publish data every 30 seconds

Explanation

Incorrect. This metric is high-resolution, so CloudWatch can technically store data as granular as 1 second. However, the metric is only published every 30 seconds. A 30-second publish interval is longer than the required 15-second detection window, so load changes could be missed between publications. Keyword tip: high resolution describes the storage granularity CloudWatch supports, but the actual publish frequency is what determines whether a fast detection window can be met.
Your answer is correct
Create a high-resolution custom Amazon CloudWatch metric for user activity data, then publish data every 5 seconds

Explanation

Correct. A high-resolution custom metric can store and report data at intervals as short as 1 second. Publishing this metric every 5 seconds gives Overlook Labs enough data points inside the 15-second detection window to notice a load spike and trigger a scaling action in time. The publish interval must always be shorter than the required detection window, not just equal to the metric's resolution capability. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for scaling or alerting inside a window measured in seconds, pair a high-resolution custom metric with a publish interval smaller than that window.

This question tests understanding of how Amazon CloudWatch custom metric resolution and publish frequency work together to support fast auto scaling decisions. Standard-resolution metrics are always aggregated to a 1-minute granularity, no matter how often data is published, so they cannot meet sub-minute detection requirements. High-resolution metrics support granularities as fine as 1 second, but resolution alone is not enough: the publish interval itself must also be shorter than the required detection window. The correct decision process has two steps: first choose high resolution whenever sub-minute detection is required, then confirm the publish interval is short enough to capture changes within the stated time window.

Business scenario: Overlook Labs runs automated experiments where researcher activity can spike suddenly when multiple lab teams start data uploads at the same time. By publishing a high-resolution custom CloudWatch metric every 5 seconds, the platform team can detect these spikes within the required 15-second window and trigger ECS task scaling before the processing service becomes overloaded.

Question 46Incorrect

Prairiewind Institute's DynamoDB table tracks gate assignments with 500 provisioned WCUs across 5 partitions. During peak boarding, one partition absorbs about 300 WCU per second while the others receive far less traffic, and writes fail with 'ProvisionedThroughputExceededException' even though aggregate capacity has headroom.

What is the likely cause?

Correct answer
You have a hot partition

Explanation

Correct. DynamoDB divides a table's data across multiple partitions based on the partition key. When many requests target the same partition key values, one partition receives much more traffic than the others. This uneven traffic pattern is called a hot partition. DynamoDB's adaptive capacity feature can shift some throughput to help a hot partition, but if traffic on that partition still exceeds its own throughput limit, DynamoDB throttles requests and returns 'ProvisionedThroughputExceededException'. Keyword tip: when one partition receives a disproportionate share of read or write traffic while the table's total provisioned capacity still has headroom, that pattern points to a hot partition, and the fix is a more distributed partition key design.
Your answer is incorrect
Write Capacity Units (WCUs) are applied across all of the account's DynamoDB tables and this needs reconfiguration

Explanation

Incorrect. DynamoDB configures Write Capacity Units (WCUs) and Read Capacity Units (RCUs) separately for each table. DynamoDB does not share these capacity settings across other tables in the same account. This statement misrepresents how DynamoDB capacity allocation works. Keyword tip: remember that DynamoDB capacity settings, whether provisioned or on-demand, apply only to one table and its indexes, never to an entire account.
CloudWatch monitoring is lagging

Explanation

Incorrect. The error 'ProvisionedThroughputExceededException' comes directly from DynamoDB. DynamoDB sends this error when provisioned capacity or partition-level throughput is exceeded. CloudWatch monitoring lag does not cause this error; CloudWatch only reports metrics, it does not enforce capacity limits. Keyword tip: if an error name references a specific AWS service's throughput or capacity, investigate that service directly, not the monitoring tool.
The configured IAM policy is incorrect

Explanation

Incorrect. An incorrectly configured IAM policy produces an authorization error, such as AccessDeniedException. IAM policies do not control DynamoDB throughput limits. The error 'ProvisionedThroughputExceededException' is tied to capacity limits, not permissions. Keyword tip: separate 'AccessDenied' style errors, which point to IAM or permissions, from 'Throughput' or 'Exceeded' style errors, which point to capacity or throttling.

DynamoDB spreads a table's items across partitions using the partition key, and provisioned capacity is set at the table level while each partition also has its own throughput ceiling. If a small number of partition key values receive most of the traffic, that single partition can hit its own limit even when the table's total provisioned capacity still has room. This pattern is called a hot partition. DynamoDB's adaptive capacity feature can redistribute some throughput automatically, but sustained traffic skew still triggers throttling and the 'ProvisionedThroughputExceededException' error. The correct fix is to redesign the partition key so that traffic spreads evenly across many distinct values; monitoring delays, account-wide capacity sharing, and IAM permissions do not cause this specific exception.

In practice: Prairiewind Institute could redesign its gate-assignment table so that the partition key combines the flight number with a shard suffix, instead of using only the airport code, which concentrates traffic during peak boarding windows at busy hubs. This change spreads write traffic across more partitions and prevents a single partition from becoming a bottleneck during high-volume travel periods.

Question 47Correct

Crestline Systems migrated its SQL Server database to an Amazon RDS instance in a private VPC subnet with no public internet exposure, and rewrote its related Java application as an AWS Lambda function. Which approach allows the Lambda function to connect to the RDS instance?

Configure the Lambda function to connect to a public subnet that will provide internet access, and use a security group to access the RDS instance inside the private subnet

Explanation

Incorrect. Attaching a Lambda function to a subnet does not automatically give the Lambda function internet access or a public IP address, even if the subnet is labeled public. Internet access requires a NAT gateway or NAT instance that the subnet's route table can reach. Connecting the Lambda function to a public subnet is unnecessary here, because the Amazon RDS instance already resides in a private subnet in the same VPC. The Lambda function should instead attach to that same private subnet with the correct security group. Keyword tip: subnet association alone never grants internet access in the Lambda VPC networking model; a NAT gateway is always required for outbound internet traffic from a private subnet.
Use Lambda layers to connect to the internet and to the RDS instance separately

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda layers are ZIP archives that package extra code, libraries, or a custom runtime for a Lambda function to use. Lambda layers do not affect networking or connectivity in any way. Only the Lambda function's VPC configuration, meaning its subnets and security groups, can create a network path to a VPC-hosted resource. Keyword tip: Lambda layers relate to code and dependency packaging, not network access, so this option should be ruled out whenever the question is about reaching a VPC resource.
Use environment variables to pass in the RDS connection string

Explanation

Incorrect. Environment variables store configuration values, such as a connection string or endpoint, that Lambda function code can read at runtime. Environment variables do not create network-level connectivity to a resource inside a VPC. Even with the correct connection string stored in an environment variable, the Lambda function would still fail to reach the Amazon RDS instance unless the Lambda function is attached to the VPC through the correct subnet and security group. Keyword tip: environment variables solve a configuration or secrets problem, not a networking problem.
Your answer is correct
Configure the Lambda function to connect to the VPC using the private subnet and the security group needed to access the RDS instance

Explanation

Correct. AWS Lambda can connect to a VPC by specifying subnets and security groups in the function's VPC configuration. When the Lambda function connects to a private subnet, AWS creates network interfaces, called elastic network interfaces, for each subnet and security group combination. These elastic network interfaces let the Lambda function reach resources like the Amazon RDS instance as if the Lambda function were another resource inside the VPC. Keyword tip: when a Lambda function must reach a resource that only exists inside a VPC, such as a private RDS instance or an ElastiCache cluster, the correct answer always involves VPC configuration with the correct subnets and security groups.

This question tests the distinction between network-level configuration and application-level configuration for AWS Lambda functions that must reach resources inside a VPC. A Lambda function gains network access to a VPC resource, such as an Amazon RDS instance in a private subnet, only by attaching the Lambda function to the VPC with the correct private subnets and security groups; this attachment lets AWS create elastic network interfaces that place the Lambda function on the same network as the RDS instance. Lambda layers solve code and dependency packaging problems, and environment variables solve configuration and secrets problems, but neither approach creates a network path to a VPC resource. Attaching a Lambda function to a public subnet also does not solve this problem, because subnet association alone never grants internet access; a NAT gateway is required for that, and a NAT gateway is unnecessary here since the target RDS instance is private.

In practice: Crestline Systems, a consumer electronics manufacturer, faces this exact situation after migrating its SQL Server database to Amazon RDS and rewriting its Java application as an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function must reach the RDS instance without exposing the database to the public internet, so the development team configures the Lambda function's VPC settings with the private subnet and security group that already allow access to the RDS instance. This approach keeps the database isolated from the internet while still letting the Lambda function query the database directly.

Question 48Incorrect

A new engineering hire at Keystone Consolidated needs to understand core Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling behaviors.

Which of the following statements about Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling are correct? (Select TWO.)

Every time you create an Auto Scaling group from an existing instance, it creates a new AMI (Amazon Machine Image)

Explanation

Incorrect. Creating an Auto Scaling group from an existing instance does not create a new Amazon Machine Image. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling copies the configuration of the existing instance into a new launch template. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling then uses that launch template to launch new instances. Keyword tip: the phrase "create an Auto Scaling group from an existing instance" maps to launch template creation, not Amazon Machine Image creation.
Your selection is correct
Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling works with both Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers

Explanation

Correct. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling integrates with Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling also integrates with Classic Load Balancers. Auto Scaling uses the health check results from these load balancers to detect and replace unhealthy instances. Keyword tip: link the phrase "Auto Scaling health checks with a load balancer" to support for Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, and Classic Load Balancers.
You cannot use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling for health checks (to replace unhealthy instances) if you are not using Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)

Explanation

Incorrect. Elastic Load Balancing is not required for Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling health checks. If you do not configure Elastic Load Balancing, Auto Scaling uses the default EC2 status check. The EC2 status check detects unhealthy instances and replaces them automatically. Keyword tip: EC2 status checks are the default health check method, and Elastic Load Balancing health checks are an optional addition that also checks application-layer responsiveness.
Correct selection
Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling cannot add a volume to an existing instance if the existing volume is approaching capacity

Explanation

Correct. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling attaches a new volume only when it launches a new instance. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling uses the volume configuration defined in the launch template or launch configuration. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling does not monitor existing volumes and does not add storage to existing instances when those volumes approach capacity. Keyword tip: Auto Scaling manages volume attachment only at launch time, not ongoing storage capacity for running instances.
Your selection is incorrect
EC2 Auto Scaling groups are regional constructs. They span across Availability Zones and AWS Regions

Explanation

Incorrect. An Auto Scaling group is a regional construct. An Auto Scaling group can span multiple Availability Zones within one AWS Region. An Auto Scaling group cannot span multiple AWS Regions. Keyword tip: remember the scope order where a Region contains Availability Zones, and an Auto Scaling group's reach stops at the Region boundary.

This question tests your understanding of the operational boundaries of Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling uses EC2 status checks by default to detect and replace unhealthy instances. When you attach a load balancer, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can also use load balancer health checks from Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, or Classic Load Balancers for more accurate application-level health detection. An Auto Scaling group is scoped to a single AWS Region and can span multiple Availability Zones within that Region, but it cannot span multiple Regions. Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling manages volume attachment only when it launches a new instance, using the launch template; it does not automatically manage storage growth on existing instances, and creating a group from an existing instance produces a launch template, not a new Amazon Machine Image.

A similar situation: Keystone Consolidated might run refinery monitoring services behind an Application Load Balancer across multiple Availability Zones in a single Region to keep production dashboards available during instance failures. A new engineer at Keystone Consolidated could mistakenly assume that Auto Scaling automatically expands storage on existing instances or spans multiple Regions, so a mentor would clarify these operational boundaries before the engineer configures a scaling policy for the company's data ingestion fleet.

Question 49Correct

Vantage Solutions needs its Dockerized microservices stored in an AWS-native container registry, with multiple tasks from a single service running on the same shared EC2 instance using dynamic port mapping. Which combination of load balancer and orchestration service meets these requirements?

Application Load Balancer + Elastic Beanstalk

Explanation

Incorrect. Elastic Beanstalk can run multiple Docker containers on one EC2 instance. However, Elastic Beanstalk gives less control over task placement and port mapping than Amazon ECS. Amazon ECS is the better fit when a scenario requires fine-grained control over container orchestration and dynamic port mapping. Keyword tip: when a scenario emphasizes fine-grained control over container orchestration and dynamic port mapping, choose Amazon ECS instead of Elastic Beanstalk.
Your answer is correct
Application Load Balancer + Amazon ECS

Explanation

Correct. Amazon ECS supports dynamic port mapping. Dynamic port mapping lets multiple tasks from the same service run on the same container instance, with each task bound to a different ephemeral port. An Application Load Balancer integrates natively with Amazon ECS, automatically registering and deregistering targets using the instance ID and the dynamic port assigned to each task. This combination meets all stated requirements. Keyword tip: the phrase "dynamic port mapping" combined with "multiple tasks on the same instance" points to Application Load Balancer plus Amazon ECS.
Classic Load Balancer + Amazon ECS

Explanation

Incorrect. A Classic Load Balancer needs static port mapping on the container instance. A Classic Load Balancer cannot register multiple copies of the same task when each copy runs on a different dynamic port on one instance. Keyword tip: a Classic Load Balancer paired with a requirement for dynamic port mapping signals that the option is wrong.
Classic Load Balancer + Elastic Beanstalk

Explanation

Incorrect. This combination fails for two reasons. First, a Classic Load Balancer cannot support dynamic port mapping and requires static port assignment. Second, Elastic Beanstalk offers less fine-grained control over container placement than Amazon ECS. Keyword tip: eliminate any option that pairs a Classic Load Balancer with a container workload that requires dynamic ports.

This question tests the relationship between load balancer type and container orchestration service when dynamic port mapping is required. Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type supports dynamic port mapping, so multiple tasks from the same service can run on one EC2 instance, each using a different ephemeral port. An Application Load Balancer is required in this case because it tracks each task's instance ID and dynamic port automatically, while a Classic Load Balancer only supports static port mapping and cannot handle multiple tasks on dynamic ports. Elastic Beanstalk can also run multiple containers on one instance through its multi-container Docker platform, but Elastic Beanstalk does not give the same level of orchestration control as Amazon ECS. The correct choice matches the load balancer type to its dynamic port mapping capability, and matches the orchestration service to the level of control the scenario requires.

Practical example: Vantage Solutions, an agricultural cooperative, is migrating its supply-chain tracking microservices to Docker containers on Amazon ECS. Vantage Solutions needs multiple tasks from the same service to run on a single EC2 instance to reduce infrastructure costs, and Vantage Solutions needs the load balancer to automatically route traffic to the correct dynamic port for each task. Pairing an Application Load Balancer with Amazon ECS meets both requirements without manual port management.

Question 50Correct

Crestline Innovations runs a nightly batch job on an EC2 instance that must pull order records from an S3 bucket without hardcoding AWS credentials on the instance. Which approach should the company use so the instance can access the data securely?

Use EC2 User Data

Explanation

Incorrect. EC2 User Data passes bootstrap scripts or configuration data to an instance. A User Data script runs when the instance launches, or on later boots if configured. User Data does not grant ongoing, secure access to AWS services like S3. Keyword tip: User Data is for instance initialization, not for identity and access management.
Your answer is correct
Use an IAM role

Explanation

Correct. An IAM role lets an application on an EC2 instance make API requests to AWS services such as S3, without long-term credentials. Amazon EC2 attaches the IAM role to the instance through an instance profile. The AWS SDK or CLI automatically retrieves temporary, auto-rotated credentials from the instance metadata service. Keyword tip: when an EC2 instance needs credential-free, auto-rotated access to AWS resources, the correct answer is an IAM role attached through an instance profile.
Create an S3 bucket policy that authorizes public access

Explanation

Incorrect. Configuring an S3 bucket policy to allow public access lets anyone on the internet read the bucket's objects. This configuration violates the requirement for secure access. Public access exposes sensitive order data to unauthorized users. Keyword tip: a public bucket policy is a red flag whenever a scenario calls for restricted or secure access.
Create an IAM programmatic user and store the access key and secret access key in the EC2 instance's ~/.aws/credentials file

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing IAM user access keys in the EC2 instance's ~/.aws/credentials file lets the application authenticate to S3. This method is insecure. Anyone who compromises the EC2 instance can steal these long-term credentials. The attacker can then reuse the stolen credentials outside the instance. Keyword tip: avoid static, long-term IAM credentials stored directly on an EC2 instance.

This question tests secure credential management for EC2 access to S3, a core AWS security best practice. An IAM role, attached to an EC2 instance through an instance profile, provides temporary, automatically rotated credentials, so no secrets need to be stored or managed. Static IAM user credentials placed on an instance create a long-lived secret that an attacker can steal and reuse outside the instance. EC2 User Data only handles instance bootstrapping and has no role in ongoing access control, while a public S3 bucket policy grants access to anyone on the internet, violating the principle of least privilege.

Use case: A telecommunications provider like Crestline Innovations runs nightly billing reconciliation jobs on EC2 instances that must read order records from S3. Attaching an IAM role to these instances lets the nightly job authenticate to S3 automatically, with credentials that rotate without any manual intervention. This approach removes the operational burden of rotating access keys across a fleet of instances and reduces the risk of credential leakage if an instance is compromised.

Question 51Correct

Mapleridge Systems runs a customer portal on Amazon API Gateway REST APIs for field technicians. It now needs to push real-time alerts to technicians from backend services without implementing polling. Which type of API supported by Amazon API Gateway meets this requirement?

REST or HTTP APIs

Explanation

Incorrect. Neither REST APIs nor HTTP APIs support a server-initiated push mechanism. Combining REST APIs and HTTP APIs does not remove the need for polling, because both still require the client to initiate every request. Keyword tip: if an answer combines two request-response API types to solve a real-time push requirement, treat it as a distractor because neither type supports persistent bidirectional connections.
HTTP APIs

Explanation

Incorrect. An HTTP API is optimized for low-latency, low-cost REST-style integrations. Examples include proxying requests to AWS Lambda or other HTTP endpoints. An HTTP API follows a request-response model, so the client must send a request before the server can respond. The server cannot push data to the client without a new request from the client. Keyword tip: HTTP APIs are for lightweight, cost-efficient proxy integrations, not for server-initiated push notifications.
REST APIs

Explanation

Incorrect. A REST API in API Gateway uses resources and methods that respond to client requests such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. Like an HTTP API, a REST API uses a synchronous request-response pattern. A REST API has no built-in way for the server to push updates to the client, so an application built on it would need to poll the server for updates. Keyword tip: REST APIs are best for full API management features such as usage plans, request validation, and private endpoints, not for real-time server push.
Your answer is correct
WebSocket APIs

Explanation

Correct. A WebSocket API keeps a single connection open between the client and the server. Both the client and the server can send messages at any time over this connection. The backend service can push data to the client as soon as an update happens. The client does not need to send repeated requests to check for updates. Keyword tip: look for words like real-time, bidirectional, or server-push in a scenario. These words point to API Gateway WebSocket APIs.

This question tests the ability to match an API Gateway API type to a communication pattern. WebSocket APIs keep a persistent, full-duplex connection open between the client and the server, and this connection lets the backend service push messages to the client in real time. REST APIs and HTTP APIs both use a synchronous, client-initiated request-response model, so an application built on either one must poll the server to detect updates. Choose WebSocket APIs for chat applications, live dashboards, and real-time alerting. Choose REST APIs when the application needs full API management features such as usage plans, API keys, and request or response transformations, and choose HTTP APIs when the application needs a lightweight, low-cost, low-latency proxy to a backend service such as AWS Lambda. The main decision driver is whether the backend needs to send data to the client without waiting for a new request.

Real-world example: Mapleridge Systems could build a WebSocket API backed by AWS Lambda to push satellite link-status alerts to field technicians as soon as a ground station reports an anomaly. This design removes the need for technicians' devices to repeatedly poll the backend for status changes, which reduces both latency and unnecessary network traffic.

Question 52Correct

At Vailmont Consolidated, developers now own the entire software delivery process from source commit through production deployment. As engineering lead, you must retain authority to manually approve any release before it proceeds.

Which approach supports this workflow?

Create multiple AWS CodePipelines for each environment and link them using AWS Lambda

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda functions can run as actions inside a CodePipeline stage. However, using AWS Lambda to link multiple separate pipelines together adds unnecessary complexity. AWS Lambda does not natively provide a manual approval capability. Manual approval is a built-in CodePipeline stage type, not something you build with a separate compute service. Keyword tip: if an option uses AWS Lambda just to connect pipelines instead of using a native pipeline feature, treat it as an overengineered workaround.
Your answer is correct
Create one AWS CodePipeline for the entire flow and add a manual approval step

Explanation

Correct. AWS CodePipeline lets you add a manual approval action to a stage in the pipeline. The pipeline pauses at that action. A designated approver, such as the engineering lead, must manually approve or reject the transition before the pipeline continues. This design lets developers build and own the full pipeline, including source, build, test, and deploy stages, while the engineering lead keeps control at a specific checkpoint. No separate pipelines or extra integration work are needed. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes one pipeline that needs a human checkpoint before moving forward, think of the manual approval action inside AWS CodePipeline.
Use AWS CodePipeline with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodePipeline supports Amazon VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink. This feature keeps pipeline API traffic inside a VPC instead of routing it over the public internet. This feature improves network security and isolation, but it does not add a manual approval checkpoint. This feature also does not change how the pipeline is modeled. Keyword tip: VPC endpoints and PrivateLink relate to network privacy, not to approval steps or workflow governance.
Create deeply integrated AWS CodePipelines for each environment

Explanation

Incorrect. Deeply integrating separate AWS CodePipelines for each environment can be a valid continuous delivery pattern. For example, a team might chain a test environment pipeline into a production deployment pipeline using AWS CloudFormation. However, this design is more complex than the scenario requires. This design does not directly provide a single, centralized manual approval checkpoint owned by the engineering lead. Keyword tip: when a simpler, single-pipeline native feature already meets the stated requirement, a multi-pipeline integration design is usually a distractor built on unnecessary complexity.

AWS CodePipeline includes a native manual approval action that pauses a pipeline at a defined stage until a designated approver accepts or rejects the transition. Use this action when a single pipeline, owned end to end by developers, needs one human checkpoint at a specific point in an otherwise automated workflow. Reserve multi-pipeline or cross-environment designs, such as chaining pipelines with AWS CloudFormation or AWS Lambda, for cases that genuinely require separate, independently managed environments rather than a simple approval gate. Amazon VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink solve network isolation and security problems, not workflow control problems, so they do not satisfy an approval requirement.

Business scenario: Vailmont Consolidated's development team owns a single delivery pipeline that automatically builds, tests, and stages updates to their solar farm monitoring dashboard. Before any update reaches production, the engineering lead must manually confirm that the release is safe, since an incorrect deployment could disrupt real-time energy production data. Adding a manual approval action to that one pipeline gives the lead this exact checkpoint without requiring a separate approval system or additional pipelines.

Question 53Correct

Orchardvale Industries has a CloudFormation deployment with three stacks. Stack-A provisions a VPC, security group, and subnets, exporting these values for Stack-B and Stack-C to import. CloudFormation blocks deleting a stack while another stack still imports its exported values.

In what order should the developer delete the three stacks?

Stack A, then Stack B, then Stack C

Explanation

Incorrect. This order deletes Stack A first. Stack A's outputs are still imported by Stack B and Stack C at that point. AWS CloudFormation will reject the deletion of Stack A because active imports still exist. Keyword tip: seeing the exporting stack listed first in a deletion sequence is a sign the order is wrong.
Stack A, Stack C, then Stack B

Explanation

Incorrect. This order tries to delete Stack A before Stack B. Stack B still imports values that Stack A exports at that point. AWS CloudFormation blocks deletion of an exporting stack while any other stack still imports its values. Keyword tip: if a stack exports a value with Fn::ImportValue used elsewhere, that exporting stack must always be deleted last.
Stack C, then Stack A, then Stack B

Explanation

Incorrect. This order deletes Stack C first, but it still places Stack A's deletion before Stack B's deletion. Stack B still imports values from Stack A at that point, so the deletion of Stack A fails. Keyword tip: the position of independent stacks in the sequence does not matter, but every importing stack must still come before the exporting stack.
Your answer is correct
Stack B, then Stack C, then Stack A

Explanation

Correct. Stack A exports the VPC, security group, and subnet values that Stack B and Stack C import. AWS CloudFormation does not allow Stack A to be deleted, or its exported outputs changed, while those imports still exist. Deleting Stack B and Stack C first removes all the imports, so Stack A can then be deleted safely. Keyword tip: always delete every importing stack before deleting the exporting stack.

This question tests the concept of cross-stack references in AWS CloudFormation. One stack exports output values using the Export field. Other stacks import those values using Fn::ImportValue. AWS CloudFormation enforces a strict rule: an exporting stack cannot be deleted, and its exported output cannot be modified, while any other stack still imports that value. Because of this rule, when tearing down a set of interdependent stacks, delete every stack that imports a value first, then delete the stack that exports the value last.

Use case: Orchardvale Industries uses this same pattern when decommissioning a temporary staging environment for its refinery monitoring portal. The network stack exports the VPC, subnet, and security group values, while separate application stacks import those values to launch their resources. Before the network stack can be removed, the developer must first delete every application stack that still imports its outputs, otherwise AWS CloudFormation rejects the deletion.

Question 54Correct

Millbrook Systems provides a public API, built with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda, that serves statistical data updated daily to anonymous external partners. Usage has grown substantially, and the company wants to improve the API's responsiveness for consumers. What should the company do?

Your answer is correct
Activate caching in API Gateway.

Explanation

Correct. Enabling caching in API Gateway lets API Gateway store responses from the backend Lambda function. API Gateway keeps these stored responses for a configurable time-to-live (TTL) period. This reduces the number of calls made to the Lambda function for repeated requests. Fewer backend calls mean lower latency and better responsiveness for API consumers. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks how to reduce backend calls and latency for frequently requested, slowly changing data served through API Gateway, think of the built-in API Gateway caching feature.
Cache API results in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon ElastiCache works well for caching data that an application retrieves from a database or another backend data store. Amazon ElastiCache is not a native caching mechanism for API Gateway responses. Using Amazon ElastiCache for this purpose would require the Lambda function to contain custom logic to check the cache, store results, and manage expiration. Keyword tip: when a question asks for API Gateway response caching without extra custom logic, the native API Gateway cache feature is the simpler and more direct solution compared to Amazon ElastiCache.
Set up API keys and usage plans in API Gateway.

Explanation

Incorrect. API keys identify individual callers. Usage plans throttle requests and enforce quotas per caller. These features support access control and fair usage management. API keys and usage plans do not cache responses and do not reduce latency. Keyword tip: usage plans and API keys signal governance and throttling requirements, not performance improvement.
Set up API Gateway with an interface VPC endpoint.

Explanation

Incorrect. An interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) restricts API access to traffic that originates inside a VPC. This keeps traffic off the public internet. An interface VPC endpoint improves network security and isolation. An interface VPC endpoint does not reduce backend processing time or response latency. Keyword tip: interface VPC endpoints signal private, secure connectivity requirements, not caching or performance improvement.

This question tests API Gateway's built-in caching feature and how it differs from other API Gateway configuration options. API Gateway caching stores backend responses for a configurable time-to-live period, which reduces the number of calls sent to the Lambda backend and lowers latency for repeated requests. API keys and usage plans control access and throttle requests, but they do not cache data or reduce latency. Interface VPC endpoints provide private network connectivity, and Amazon ElastiCache provides general-purpose caching inside the application's own architecture, but neither one directly reduces API Gateway response latency without extra integration work.

Use case: A petrochemical company like Millbrook Systems might publish daily commodity pricing statistics through a public API that many external partners poll frequently throughout the day. Enabling API Gateway caching lets most of these repeated requests get served from the cache instead of invoking the Lambda function each time. This reduces both response latency and Lambda invocation costs, and the caching layer scales automatically as more consumers query the same daily dataset.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-caching.html

Question 55Incorrect

Cascade Alliance has a REST API on Amazon API Gateway in us-west-2. An external partner requires access through a custom domain name secured with an SSL/TLS certificate purchased from a third-party certificate authority. What is the appropriate strategy for configuring the custom domain name?

Correct answer
Import the third-party SSL/TLS certificate to AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), link it with the custom domain name in API Gateway, and then create an alias (A) record in Route 53 for the custom domain name.

Explanation

Correct. The third-party certificate must first be imported into ACM, because API Gateway custom domain names only accept certificates that are managed through ACM. After the certificate is associated with the custom domain name in API Gateway, an alias (A) record in Route 53 is created to point to the API Gateway domain name. Alias records support AWS service endpoints natively and do not add extra DNS lookup costs. Keyword tip: the phrase "import into ACM, then create an alias record" describes the standard pattern for setting up a custom domain on API Gateway.
Use the third-party SSL/TLS certificate directly with Amazon CloudFront, bypass API Gateway, and create an alias (A) record in Route 53.

Explanation

Incorrect. An API Gateway edge-optimized custom domain is backed by a CloudFront distribution that AWS manages internally. A developer cannot configure a separate CloudFront distribution directly and bypass the API Gateway custom domain feature. The SSL/TLS certificate must still be imported into ACM and associated with the API Gateway custom domain name, not applied directly to an unrelated CloudFront distribution. Keyword tip: any option that suggests "bypassing" API Gateway to configure CloudFront directly describes an unsupported workaround.
Your answer is incorrect
Directly install the third-party SSL/TLS certificate on the API Gateway and establish a CNAME record in Route 53 for the custom domain name.

Explanation

Incorrect. API Gateway does not allow a third-party certificate to be installed directly on the API. The certificate must be imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) before it can be attached to a custom domain name. Route 53 also recommends using an alias (A) record instead of a CNAME record when the target is an AWS-managed endpoint like API Gateway, because a CNAME record cannot be used at the zone apex and does not support AWS routing optimizations. Keyword tip: any option that describes installing a certificate directly on API Gateway, without mentioning ACM, is a distractor.
Use Route 53 to create a simple routing policy with the custom domain name directly pointed to the API Gateway.

Explanation

Incorrect. A Route 53 simple routing policy using a standard record cannot resolve directly to an API Gateway endpoint. The custom domain name resource in API Gateway must be configured first, and a validated certificate must be associated with it. Route 53 alias records, not simple non-alias records, are required to point to this custom domain name. Keyword tip: any option that skips the API Gateway custom domain name setup step is missing a required configuration step.

Setting up a custom domain for API Gateway with a third-party certificate requires three steps in a fixed order: import the certificate into ACM, attach it to the custom domain name resource in API Gateway, and create an alias record in Route 53 pointing to the API Gateway domain name. Use ACM certificate import when the certificate already comes from an external certificate authority. Use ACM certificate issuance instead when AWS should manage the certificate lifecycle, including renewal. Always prefer alias records over CNAME records for AWS-managed endpoints, because alias records work at the zone apex and avoid extra DNS resolution steps.

Applied example: Cascade Alliance's engineering team needs external lab partners to reach its research data API through a branded domain name, such as api.cascadealliance.com, while keeping the SSL/TLS certificate the company already purchased from its existing certificate authority. By importing that certificate into ACM, attaching it to the API Gateway custom domain name, and then creating a Route 53 alias record, the team meets the partner's security requirement without purchasing a new AWS-issued certificate or re-architecting the existing API Gateway deployment.

Question 56Incorrect

Dovetail Systems uses a cron job to poll for new wire transfer orders and sends each order to message queues for downstream processing. The company wants to migrate this to AWS to eliminate polling and reliably deliver each order to multiple independent downstream consumers.

Which solution is most optimal?

Correct answer
Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) to push notifications when an order is created. Configure different Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) queues to receive these messages for downstream processing

Explanation

Correct. This is the SNS-to-SQS fanout pattern. SNS pushes a notification as soon as a new order is created, which removes the need for a polling cron job. Multiple SQS queues subscribed to the SNS topic each durably store a copy of the message, so independent downstream consumers can process the order reliably and asynchronously. Keyword tip: a push notification combined with multiple independent downstream consumers that each need a reliable, durable copy of the message is the signature of an SNS-to-SQS fanout architecture.
Your answer is incorrect
Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) to push notifications to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery streams for processing the data for downstream applications

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SNS can publish messages to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Kinesis Data Firehose is built for near-real-time streaming of large data volumes into analytics destinations, such as Amazon S3 or Amazon Redshift. Kinesis Data Firehose is not built for reliable, decoupled processing between order-handling components, and it costs more than SQS for this type of workload. Keyword tip: when a question mentions streaming analytics or delivery to a data lake, think Kinesis Data Firehose. When a question mentions decoupling and reliable message processing between application components, think SQS.
Configure different Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) queues to poll for new orders

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS is a pull-based queue service. A consumer must poll the queue to retrieve messages. SQS does not poll external systems to detect new events on its own. A producer must actively send a message into the queue before any consumer can retrieve it. Keyword tip: SQS consumers poll the queue for messages, but SQS cannot poll upstream systems to discover new orders by itself.
Use Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) to push notifications and use AWS Lambda functions to process the information received from SNS

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SNS can invoke an AWS Lambda function directly when a message is published. Lambda has no built-in mechanism to durably store a message if a function invocation fails. This creates a risk of message loss. The scenario requires reliable, decoupled processing with message persistence, which calls for a durable queue like SQS instead of direct Lambda invocation. Keyword tip: when a question emphasizes reliability and message retention after a failure, prefer an SNS-to-SQS fanout over a direct SNS-to-Lambda subscription.

This question tests understanding of the SNS-to-SQS fanout pattern for replacing an inefficient polling architecture with an event-driven, decoupled messaging design. Use Amazon SNS when you need to push a notification to multiple subscribers immediately after an event occurs. Use Amazon SQS when you need durable, reliable message storage so one or more downstream consumers can process a message asynchronously, even if a consumer is temporarily unavailable. Combining SNS and SQS lets a single event fan out to multiple independently scalable queues without losing any messages, which is different from direct SNS-to-Lambda invocation, since Lambda has no built-in message durability, and different from Kinesis Data Firehose, which targets streaming analytics rather than transactional order processing.

Applied example: Dovetail Systems processes wire transfer orders that must reach several independent downstream systems, such as fraud screening, core banking ledger updates, and customer notifications. Instead of a cron job polling for new orders, Dovetail Systems can publish an event to an SNS topic the moment an order is created. Separate SQS queues, one for each downstream system, subscribe to that topic, so each system receives and processes its own durable copy of the message independently, without any risk of losing a wire transfer record if one downstream system is briefly unavailable.

Question 57Incorrect

Pinegrove Ventures runs its device telemetry API on Amazon ECS and must securely store configuration values, such as third-party API authentication tokens and endpoint URLs, separately for each deployment environment. The solution must require minimal changes to the existing application code.

Which approach meets this requirement?

Correct answer
Configure the application to fetch the variables and credentials from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store by leveraging hierarchical unique paths in Parameter Store for each variable in each of Pinegrove Ventures' environments

Explanation

Correct. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store stores configuration data and secrets securely. Parameter Store supports hierarchical paths, so Pinegrove Ventures can organize each variable under a unique path for each environment. The application retrieves these values by name at runtime using the AWS SDK. This approach requires minimal code changes because the application only calls the Parameter Store API instead of hardcoding values. Keyword tip: 'hierarchical paths for configuration or secrets across environments' points directly to Parameter Store.
Your answer is incorrect
Configure the application to fetch the variables from each of Pinegrove Ventures' deployed environments by defining the authentication information and API URL in the ECS task definition as unique names during the deployment process

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing authentication information and the API URL directly inside the ECS task definition is not secure. The task definition is visible to any IAM principal that has the DescribeTaskDefinition permission. This means the credentials would be exposed in plaintext to more users than intended. AWS recommends injecting secrets from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store or AWS Secrets Manager into the task definition instead of hardcoding the values there. Keyword tip: 'values embedded directly in the task definition' signals a security exposure, not a valid secrets-management pattern.
Configure the application to fetch the variables from AWS KMS by storing the API URL and credentials as unique keys in KMS for each environment

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS KMS manages cryptographic keys. AWS KMS does not store arbitrary configuration data or credentials as retrievable values. AWS KMS is designed for encryption and decryption operations, not for storing named string values like URLs or credentials. Keyword tip: when a question describes storing and retrieving named values such as URLs or credentials, KMS is a distractor because its purpose is key management, not value storage.
Configure the application to fetch the variables from an encrypted file that is stored with the application by storing the API URL and credentials in unique files for each environment

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing credentials in an encrypted file that is bundled with the application deployment package is not a security best practice. This approach couples secrets to the application artifact. This approach also makes credential rotation harder and increases the risk of accidental exposure through version control or deployment logs. Keyword tip: 'secrets stored in files shipped with the application' is a red flag for weak secrets handling compared to a managed secrets service.

This question tests knowledge of secure configuration and secrets management for containerized applications running on Amazon ECS. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store stores configuration values and secrets centrally, and it supports hierarchical paths that let a team organize the same variable name under a different path for each environment. AWS Secrets Manager is a similar service, but it adds automatic rotation and is typically chosen when secrets need to rotate on a schedule. Task definitions expose environment variables in plaintext to any principal with the DescribeTaskDefinition permission, AWS KMS manages encryption keys rather than storing arbitrary values, and files bundled with the application couple secrets to the deployment artifact and complicate rotation. The correct choice depends on recognizing which service is designed to store and retrieve named values securely, rather than misusing a key-management service or hardcoding values into deployment configuration.

A similar situation: an IoT device manufacturer like Pinegrove Ventures often needs its ECS-based backend services to authenticate against multiple third-party APIs, with different endpoint URLs and credentials for development, staging, and production. By storing each variable under a hierarchical path in Parameter Store, such as /pinegrove-ventures/production/api-url, the operations team can update a credential in one environment without touching the application code or redeploying the container.

Question 58Incorrect

Fairmount Guild gives each franchise partner read-only IAM access to only their own files in a shared Amazon S3 bucket. An audit found that some S3 requests use unencrypted connections. The company must enforce encryption in transit for all requests to the bucket. Which solution meets this requirement?

Correct answer
Update the S3 bucket policy to include a condition that requires aws:SecureTransport for all actions.

Explanation

Correct. Adding a Deny statement to the bucket policy with a condition on the aws:SecureTransport key blocks any request that arrives over an unencrypted HTTP connection. This condition evaluates to false when a request does not use HTTPS, and the Deny statement then rejects that request regardless of the caller's identity or permissions. This method is the standard AWS mechanism for enforcing in-transit encryption on an S3 bucket. Keyword tip: the aws:SecureTransport condition key in a bucket policy is the specific signal that identifies the correct way to enforce encrypted connections to Amazon S3.
Enable the Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration feature to ensure encryption during transit.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration uses the Amazon CloudFront global edge network to speed up long-distance uploads and downloads. The accelerated endpoint does use HTTPS, but enabling Transfer Acceleration does not force every request to the bucket to use an encrypted connection. Transfer Acceleration solves a performance problem, not a security enforcement problem. Keyword tip: Transfer Acceleration relates to upload and download speed, not to enforcing a security requirement.
Activate Amazon S3 server-side encryption to enforce encryption during transit.

Explanation

Incorrect. Server-side encryption protects data while it is stored in Amazon S3. Server-side encryption does not protect data while it travels over the network between a client and Amazon S3. In-transit protection and at-rest protection are two separate features, and enabling one does not enable the other. Keyword tip: if an option proposes server-side encryption to solve an in-transit encryption requirement, treat it as a distractor that confuses encryption at rest with encryption in transit.
Your answer is incorrect
Assign IAM roles enforcing SSL/TLS encryption to each franchise partner.

Explanation

Incorrect. IAM roles and IAM policies control who can perform which actions on which resources. This control is called authorization. IAM roles do not force a client to use SSL/TLS when connecting to Amazon S3. Keyword tip: IAM constructs manage permissions, not the transport protocol used for the connection.

This question tests the distinction between encryption at rest, encryption in transit, and access control, along with the specific AWS mechanism used to enforce each one. Server-side encryption and AWS KMS protect data at rest. IAM policies and IAM roles control authorization, meaning who can perform which action. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration improves transfer speed over long distances but does not enforce encrypted connections. To enforce encryption in transit for Amazon S3, the correct method is to add a Deny statement to the bucket policy that triggers when the aws:SecureTransport condition key evaluates to false. This Deny statement rejects any non-HTTPS request no matter who is making it.

Practical example: a hotel chain like Fairmount Guild shares reservation and billing data with many independent franchise partners through a single S3 bucket. An audit finding that some requests use unencrypted HTTP connections is a common trigger for adding an aws:SecureTransport condition to the bucket policy, since this condition applies uniformly to every partner without requiring changes to each partner's individual IAM permissions.

Question 59Correct

Packaging code and dependencies for application-specific AWS Lambda functions as container images, then hosting those images on Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), requires meeting several Lambda-specific technical constraints.

Palisade Networks, a media streaming company based in Austin, is preparing to migrate its video-transcoding functions to this container image workflow. Which of the following statements are correct regarding this requirement? (Select TWO.)

Your selection is correct
To deploy a container image to Lambda, the container image must implement the Lambda Runtime API

Explanation

Correct. A container image must implement the Lambda Runtime API to run as a Lambda function. The Runtime API handles communication between the function code and the Lambda service during each invocation. AWS provides open-source runtime interface clients that implement this API. A developer can add one of these clients to any preferred base image to make that image Lambda-compatible. Keyword tip: the phrase "must implement the Runtime API" is the defining requirement for any custom or third-party base image used with Lambda.
Lambda supports both Windows and Linux-based container images

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda supports only Linux-based container images. Lambda does not support Windows-based container images for Lambda functions. Any base image used for a Lambda container must be based on a supported Linux distribution. Keyword tip: if an option claims Lambda supports Windows containers, treat that option as incorrect, because Lambda container support is Linux-only.
Your selection is correct
AWS Lambda does not support Lambda functions that use multi-architecture container images

Explanation

Correct. AWS provides multi-architecture base images for Lambda, but this only means the base image contains variants for different architectures. A single container image that is actually built and deployed to a Lambda function must target one specific architecture, either x86_64 or arm64, not both at the same time. Keyword tip: the phrase "multi-architecture container image" combined with "not supported" signals this exact limitation.
You can deploy a Lambda function as a container image, with a maximum size of 20 GB

Explanation

Incorrect. The maximum size for a Lambda container image, including all layers, is 10 GB, not 20 GB. This limit applies to the total uncompressed size of the image. Keyword tip: remember 10 GB as the container image size ceiling for Lambda deployments; this is a different number from the 250 MB unzipped limit that applies to .zip deployment packages.
You can test the containers locally using the Lambda Runtime API

Explanation

Incorrect. Local testing of Lambda container images uses the Lambda Runtime Interface Emulator (RIE). The RIE is a separate tool. It is not the Lambda Runtime API. The Runtime API is the interface a container image implements to communicate with the Lambda service at invocation time. The RIE emulates the Lambda execution environment on a local machine, so a developer can run and test the image before deployment. Keyword tip: the phrase "test locally" points to the Runtime Interface Emulator, while the phrase "implement the interface for invocation" points to the Runtime API.

This question tests knowledge of AWS Lambda container image support. It focuses on two areas. First, it tests the distinction between the Lambda Runtime API and the Lambda Runtime Interface Emulator. The Runtime API is the interface a container image must implement to run on Lambda. The Runtime Interface Emulator is a separate tool used only for local testing. Second, it tests operational limits: the 10 GB maximum image size, Linux-only operating system support, and the restriction that a deployed image must target a single architecture rather than multiple architectures at once. When deploying a Lambda function as a container image, always confirm that the image implements the Runtime API through a runtime interface client, targets one supported architecture, stays within the 10 GB size limit, and is based on a supported Linux distribution.

Practical example: Palisade Networks packages its custom video-transcoding logic as a container image so it can reuse existing Docker tooling and larger dependency libraries than a .zip deployment package would allow. Before deployment, the engineering team confirms the image implements the Lambda Runtime API through the appropriate runtime interface client, builds the image for a single target architecture, and keeps the image under the 10 GB size limit so the function deploys successfully on Amazon ECR and Lambda.
